docs.title: scMultiBench
docs.text:
A systematic benchmark of single-cell multimodal integration. Run 40+ integration methods through one typed Python API, score them with scIB and task-specific metrics, and explore the rankings to pick the right method for your data. 

pip install multibench-sc

Get started How it works

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
The scMultiBench API (imported as multibench, aliased throughout the docs as mtb) exposes a small, flat, free-function API organised into a handful of namespaces:

  • mtb.* - the top-level surface: the benchmark workflow (scan, plan, run_all, describe_layout), run one method, evaluate an output, to_long to reshape it, stored results (load_results, results_coverage, recommend), and discovery helpers (list_methods, find_methods, method_info, cite, inputs_for, labels_for, runtime_hint).
  • mtb.plot.* - scIB-style figures (bubble, bar).
  • mtb.eval.* - the evaluation pipeline (evaluate, to_long).
  • mtb.io.* - the canonical-format adapter (export_dataset, from_mudata, to_canonical, write_labels, read_canonical).
  • mtb.data.* - fetch the reference datasets.
  • mtb.catalog.* - typed views of the benchmark's metadata tables.
  • mtb.config.* - resolved paths and on-disk token maps.
  • mtb.env.* - per-method conda environments: status, plan, provisioning.

The end-to-end story: mtb.io.export_dataset writes your data as a dataset folder, mtb.scan says which methods can run on it, mtb.run_all runs and scores them into a BatchResult whose .long frame - the same tidy frame mtb.load_results returns for the stored benchmark - goes into mtb.plot.bubble. Underneath, mtb.run returns a RunResult whose output flows into mtb.evaluate, and mtb.to_long reshapes that into the same long frame. The same story from the shell:

terminal
multibench layout vertical                         # how to lay out MY data
multibench convert my.h5ad data/MYCITE --rna X --adt obsm:protein --labels obs:celltype
multibench scan MYCITE --category vertical --data-path data
multibench run --method Matilda --category vertical --input rna=... --out-dir runs/Matilda
multibench evaluate --output runs/Matilda/embedding.h5 --labels data/MYCITE/cty.csv \
    --method Matilda --dataset MYCITE --category vertical --out runs/Matilda/long.csv
multibench plot bubble --category vertical --dataset D11 --out fig.pdf
multibench cite Matilda MOFA2

Every subcommand wraps exactly one Python function with the same flag names; multibench <command> --help documents every flag. Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 a runtime error (error: ... on stderr; MULTIBENCH_DEBUG=1 shows the traceback), 2 a usage error.

Method environments

Running a method shells out to the conda environment it shares with other compatible tools via conda run -n <env> <cmd>, where <env> is mtb.env.group_for(method) - the same env multibench env install provisions (overridable through cmd_template). The original method scripts are never modified - multibench only builds the command, converts inputs to the canonical .h5, and loads the typed output.

Error vocabulary

Every entry point validates its tokens the same way: an unknown method id raises KeyError with a did-you-mean hint; an unknown category, task, atac or modality token raises ValueError listing the valid values; a missing dataset folder raises FileNotFoundError listing the folders that exist. Nothing silently returns an empty result.

docs.title: Benchmark workflow
docs.text: The four category tutorials are built on these functions.

docs.title: mtb.scan
docs.text:
mtb.scan(dataset: str, category: str | None = None, data_path: Path | str | None = None, *,
         methods: list[str] | None = None, modalities: list[str] | None = None,
         verbose: bool = False) -> pd.DataFrame

Report every method that can run on dataset, and why the rest cannot. One row per (method, category, modalities) variant with two independent gates:

  • files_ok / files_reason - the input files resolve on disk, are oriented features x cells, every label CSV has one row per cell of the modality it labels, and a data_dir method finds what it needs (>= 2 .h5ad slices with obsm['spatial'] for registration). This gate always runs, whether or not any conda env is installed - a laptop without environments still tells you whether your layout is right.
  • env_ok / env_reason - the method's conda env exists on this machine; the reason names the env and the one-method install command.

runnable = files_ok & env_ok; reason joins the non-empty reasons (empty iff runnable). Further columns: modalities (a +-joined string here, e.g. "rna+adt"; run_all / inputs_for take a list - split on "+"; "(data_dir)" marks a method that consumes a whole directory), env, output_kind, n_tunable, needs_labels (does this variant demand a label file), atac ('peak' / 'gene_activity' / None), runtime_tier / observed_worst_sec (measured, see runtime_hint) and caveat (known content traps, e.g. an atac_gas role that fell back to a peak matrix). Nothing is executed.

Parameters

  • dataset (str) - folder NAME under data_path (not a path); a missing folder raises FileNotFoundError listing the folders that do exist.
  • category (str | None) - restrict to one category (ValueError on a typo); default all four.
  • data_path (Path | str | None) - the folder that CONTAINS dataset; default the configured data root.
  • methods (list[str] | None, keyword-only) - restrict to these ids (KeyError with a hint on a typo); blocked rows are kept with their reason.
  • modalities (list[str] | None, keyword-only) - restrict to one modality combination (["rna", "adt"]; protein accepted for adt).
  • verbose (bool) - print [scan] files OK for k/n method rows; e/n envs installed.

docs.title: mtb.plan
docs.text:
mtb.plan(dataset: str, category: str, *, methods: list[str] | None = None,
         modalities: list[str] | None = None, data_path: Path | str | None = None,
         verbose: bool = False) -> pd.DataFrame

What run_all WOULD attempt - exactly the frame run_all(..., dry_run=True) returns, without an out_dir: scan restricted to methods / modalities, runnable rows first, blocked rows kept with reason and the files_ok / env_ok columns. Never empty: ValueError when no variant of the requested methods exists under category. Filter plan[plan.runnable] for what will actually run.

docs.title: mtb.run_all
docs.text:
mtb.run_all(dataset: str, category: str, *, out_dir, modalities=None, methods=None,
            params: dict | None = None, data_path=None, evaluate: bool = True,
            dry_run: bool = False, verbose: bool = True, timeout: float | None = None,
            skip_existing: bool = False, batch=None) -> BatchResult   # DataFrame when dry_run=True

Run every method that scan marks runnable (or the methods= subset) on dataset end to end - inputs, the method's own conda env, output loading, metrics - and collect everything in a BatchResult. A method that fails becomes a row in .failures, never an exception.

Parameters

  • dataset / data_path - as in scan.
  • out_dir - one sub-directory per method; ignored (may be None) when dry_run=True.
  • methods (list[str] | None) - restrict to these ids (KeyError + hint on a typo).
  • modalities (list[str] | None) - restrict to ONE modality combination, e.g. ["rna", "atac_gas"] (gene activity) vs ["rna", "atac_peak"] (peaks). The two ATAC representations do NOT map to the obvious filenames - see describe_layout.
  • params (dict | None) - per-method hyperparameters, {"Cobolt": {"lr": 1e-3}}; discover them with params_for.
  • dry_run (bool) - return the plan (a DataFrame, see plan) without running anything. Free; do it first.
  • timeout (float | None) - per-method wall-clock cap in seconds; size it from scan's runtime_tier / observed_worst_sec. A method exceeding it is recorded as TIMEOUT and the sweep moves on.
  • skip_existing (bool) - reuse a method's existing output file instead of recomputing (resume an interrupted sweep). Together with params= it raises ValueError - reuse is keyed on the file, not the parameters. Reuse only checks that the file exists, not that it is complete.
  • batch (keyword-only) - one batch id per cell, in the embedding's row order (array-like / Series / CSV path), used for the batch metrics INSTEAD of the default rule (batch = the label FILE each cell came from, cty1.csv -> 1 ...). Recorded as batch_source='user'; a wrong length marks that method RUN_OK_EVAL_FAILED.
  • evaluate (bool) - compute metrics on the outputs (default True); verbose - per-method progress lines.

docs.title: BatchResult
docs.text:
What run_all returns (and load_batch reloads).

  • .summary - one row per method, sorted by method name: method, status, run_sec, output_kind, emb_shape, n_tunable, label_order, label_order_confidence, batch_source, n_batches plus one column per metric. status is CHAIN_OK, CHAIN_OK_GRAPH_METHOD, RUN_OK_NO_EMBEDDING, RUN_OK_EVAL_FAILED, TIMEOUT or FAIL; batch_source is file_of_origin (the label-file rule), user (batch= / rescore) or None (single label file).
  • .long - the tidy metric, value, method, dataset, category frame - the input to mtb.plot.bubble.
  • .failures - method, status, error for everything that went wrong (always check it).
  • .results - the raw per-method records (status, out_dir, metrics, label_order_candidates), so a sweep's outputs stay addressable.
  • .plot(**kw) - bubble figure of every scored method; keywords go to plot.bubble (metrics=, methods=, order=, title=, save= ...). Raises ValueError if nothing scored.
  • .rescore(*, batch=None, labels=None, only=None, verbose=False) -> BatchResult - re-evaluate the STORED outputs with a different batch vector, labels or metric subset - nothing is re-run; returns a new BatchResult (call .save() to persist it).
  • .save(out_dir=None) -> Path - writes summary.csv, long.csv, failures.csv, batch_result.json (run_all does this automatically).

docs.title: mtb.load_batch
docs.text:
mtb.load_batch(out_dir) -> BatchResult

Reload a BatchResult that run_all / BatchResult.save wrote, to re-plot, re-inspect or rescore without re-running anything.

docs.title: mtb.params_for
docs.text:
mtb.params_for(method: str, category: str | None = None, modalities: list[str] | set[str] | None = None) -> dict

The tunable hyperparameters a method's variant exposes (tunable, with defaults), the defaults the wrapper emits, and the fixed arguments it controls. Multi-variant methods need modalities= to pick the variant; an empty tunable means the upstream script hardcodes its settings.

docs.title: mtb.describe_layout
docs.text:
mtb.describe_layout(category: str | None = None) -> str

How to lay out your OWN dataset so the package can find it: the directory layout and the role -> filename mapping (rna.h5, adt.h5, atac.h5 / peak.h5, cty.csv, numbered rna1.h5 ... per batch), the HDF5 file format (matrix/data features x cells, matrix/features, matrix/barcodes), the ATAC peak-vs-gene-activity warning with the method lists built from the registry at call time, the export_dataset route, and - for cross - the SPATIAL REGISTRATION block (a directory of .h5ad slices). category is validated; 'spatial' raises with a pointer to describe_layout('cross').

docs.title: mtb.runtime_hint
docs.text:
mtb.runtime_hint(method: str) -> dict

What this method has been OBSERVED to cost: {"tier", "worst_sec", "observed"} - tier in fast (<5 min), medium (5-30 min), slow (30 min-2 h), very_slow (>2 h); observed lists the actual (dataset, cells, seconds) measurements on one shared machine. Use it to size run_all(timeout=...), not to promise a finish time.

docs.title: mtb.sweep
docs.text:
mtb.sweep(dataset: str, category: str, method: str, param: str, values, *,
          out_dir, modalities=None, data_path=None, timeout=None, verbose=True) -> pd.DataFrame

Run ONE method repeatedly over a range of one hyperparameter, one output directory per value, and return the per-setting metrics with the swept value as a column (a tidy frame goes to <out_dir>/sweep_long.csv, one series per setting, ready for plot.bubble). A failing setting appears with status FAIL / TIMEOUT rather than aborting the sweep.

docs.title: mtb.run
docs.text:
mtb.run(method: str, category: str, task: str = "clustering", *, inputs: dict, out_dir: str,
        params: dict | None = None, convert: bool = True, cmd_template: str | None = None,
        repo_path: Path | None = None) -> RunResult

Build a method variant's command, preflight its conda env, wrap the command (default "conda run -n {env} {cmd}"), run it in out_dir, and load the typed output. inputs is a {modality_role: path-or-AnnData} dict; non-canonical modality inputs are auto-converted to the canonical scMultiBench .h5 (into <out_dir>/inputs/) unless convert=False. Auxiliary roles (data_dir, source_data, target_data, source_cty, target_cty, out_dir) are passed through verbatim. Returns a RunResult.

Parameters

  • method (str) - registry method id (KeyError with a did-you-mean hint otherwise).
  • category (str) - one of vertical, diagonal, mosaic, cross; drives variant selection together with the supplied modalities.
  • task (str) - reserved for future per-task dispatch; not used for variant selection in v1.
  • inputs (dict) - {modality_role: path}, e.g. {"rna": ..., "atac_gas": ...}; the non-auxiliary, non-label roles select the variant.
  • out_dir (str) - working directory; created if missing. Use an absolute path.
  • params (dict | None) - extra method hyperparameters merged into the command.
  • convert (bool) - convert non-aux inputs to the canonical .h5 (default True).
  • cmd_template (str | None) - command wrapper; None uses the method's env via conda run -n {env} {cmd} and preflights it (EnvironmentError naming the install command when the env is missing); a custom template skips the preflight.
  • repo_path (Path | None) - checkout holding tools_scripts/; default auto-provisioned (config.DEFAULT.repo_path).

docs.title: mtb.evaluate
docs.text:
mtb.evaluate(output, category: str | None = None, task: str = "clustering", labels=None,
             clustering=None, batch=None, metric_set: str = "scib", slow_metrics: bool = False,
             only=None, *, obsm: str = "X_emb", column: str | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame

Compute scIB metrics on a run output, returning a metric.csv-shaped frame (index = metric, single Value column). v1 supports metric_set="scib" with task in {clustering, batch, all} (dimension_reduction is served by the clustering group). Clustering metrics require labels; clustering is optional (omitted -> scIB optimal-resolution Leiden, ten resolutions 0.2-2.0, highest NMI). batch / all additionally require batch - unless labels is a list of two or more files, in which case the file of origin is the batch (the run_all rule). This is re-exported from mtb.eval.evaluate.

Parameters

  • output - the embedding, cells x dims: numpy.ndarray (dims x cells is auto-transposed against the label count, with a warning), pandas.DataFrame, AnnData (uses .obsm[obsm]), scipy sparse, or a path - .h5 (dataset data, the benchmark's embedding.h5), .h5ad, .npy, .csv / .tsv.
  • category (str | None) - validated when given (ValueError listing the four); metrics do not depend on it in v1.
  • task (str) - clustering (default), batch, or all.
  • labels - one cell type per cell in the row order of output: a CSV path (header row; column x / the only column / the last of two behind a barcode index - column= disambiguates), a LIST of CSV paths concatenated in order, a one-entry dict from labels_for, a 1-D array / Series / Categorical / list, a single-column DataFrame, or - for an AnnData output - an obs column name.
  • clustering - optional precomputed cluster assignment (same forms; an .h5 path is read from /obs/cluster_leiden); skips the Leiden sweep.
  • batch - batch labels, one per cell (same forms; obs column name for AnnData).
  • metric_set (str) - only "scib" is wired in v1.
  • slow_metrics (bool) - also compute kBET (shells out to R; hours on large datasets).
  • only - collection of metric names to compute ({"ARI", "NMI"}); everything else is skipped, including the Leiden sweep when no requested metric needs it. A bare string raises TypeError; unknown names raise ValueError listing mtb.plot.CLUSTERING_METRICS + mtb.plot.BATCH_METRICS.
  • obsm (str, keyword-only) - .obsm key for AnnData / .h5ad output (default "X_emb"; "X" means .X).
  • column (str | None, keyword-only) - column to take when labels is a CSV / DataFrame with several columns.

Raises ValueError for missing labels / batch, unknown category or metric name, length mismatches (input length mismatch: emb has N cells, celltype has M) and ambiguous label files; TypeError for unsupported input types.

Graceful degradation

Metrics whose external dependency is unavailable return NaN with a warning rather than failing the call: cLISI / iLISI need scib's compiled LISI helper (the warning carries the g++ rebuild command), and kBET needs R via rpy2 (and slow_metrics=True). All other scIB metrics (ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1, ASW_batch, GC) compute in pure Python.

docs.title: mtb.to_long
docs.text:
mtb.to_long(value_df, method, dataset, category) -> pd.DataFrame

Reshape an evaluate wide frame (index = metric, column Value) into the long frame (metric, value, method, dataset, category) that load_results and plot.bubble consume, canonicalising metric codes (ari -> ARI, kbet -> kBET); blank names are dropped and two rows that collapse onto the same canonical name raise ValueError (a silent duplicate would double-count that metric in every rank). Also available as mtb.eval.to_long.

docs.title: mtb.load_results
docs.text:
mtb.load_results(category: str | None = None, task: str | None = None, metric_set: str = "scib",
                 dataset: str | list[str] | None = None, method: str | list[str] | None = None,
                 metric: list[str] | str | None = None, clustering: str = "default",
                 result_path: Path | str | None = None, *, source: str = "published",
                 methods: list[str] | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame

Benchmark metric tables as a tidy long frame with the columns, in this order, metric, value, method, dataset, category, clustering, source. Method ids are canonical registry tokens (MOFA+ -> MOFA2, Seurat(WNN) -> Seurat_WNN) and metric codes canonical (iFI -> iF1). When the default-clustering correction file metric_asw_iasw_if1.csv is present, its corrected ASW / iASW / iF1 values override those in metric.csv.

Parameters

  • category (str | None) - vertical, diagonal, mosaic, or cross; None loads every category that has tables for source (ValueError on an unknown token).
  • task (str | None) - None / "all" (every metric), "clustering" (ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1, cLISI) or "batch" (ASW_batch, GC, iLISI, kBET); anything else raises.
  • metric_set (str) - only "scib" is wired (NotImplementedError otherwise).
  • dataset (str | list[str] | None) - dataset id(s); default all of the category. A dataset with no table raises FileNotFoundError naming the available ones.
  • method / methods (str | list[str] | None) - keep only these methods (alias tolerant); nothing matching gives an empty frame plus a UserWarning listing the methods present. methods= is the list alias; passing both raises.
  • metric (list[str] | str | None) - keep only these metric codes (alias tolerant; same empty-frame rule).
  • clustering (str) - default, louvain, or kmeans (metric.csv / metric_louvain.csv / metric_kmeans.csv). A <method>_louvain result dir is reported under the canonical id with clustering="louvain". The re-run sweeps are default only.
  • result_path (Path | str | None) - a results ROOT (holding scib_metric/ and/or rerun/; default the tables shipped in the package) OR a single long CSV file (then source is ignored and the frame's source column is whatever the file carries, "user" if none).
  • source (str, keyword-only) - "published" (default; the paper's scIB tables - none for mosaic), "rerun" (the package's sweeps rerun/long_all_<dataset>.csv: vertical D11/D11s, diagonal D28/D28s, mosaic D45/D45s, cross D52/D52s; source="rerun-<version>"), or "both".

Raises FileNotFoundError (no table for the request, with the path looked at and what IS available - mosaic says "use source='rerun'"), ValueError (unknown category / task / clustering / source, or a result_path file without the long-format columns).

docs.title: mtb.available_datasets
docs.text:
mtb.available_datasets(category: str | None = None, metric_set: str = "scib",
                       result_path: Path | str | None = None, *,
                       source: str = "published", clustering: str = "default") -> list[str]

The dataset ids that have a stored table for category / source / clustering - exactly what load_results can load ([] with a warning when the root is absent).

docs.title: mtb.results_coverage
docs.text:
mtb.results_coverage(category: str | None = None, *, source: str = "both",
                     result_path: Path | str | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame

Which (category, dataset, method, clustering, source) combinations have results, one row each, sorted - the published tree is scanned for every clustering variant. A category without tables simply has no rows.

docs.title: mtb.recommend
docs.text:
mtb.recommend(category: str, *, modalities: list[str] | None = None, task: str | None = "clustering",
              long_df: pd.DataFrame | None = None, metrics: list[str] | None = None,
              min_methods: int = 2, source: str = "published",
              result_path: Path | str | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame

Rank methods for a category from stored results, best first, with coverage made explicit: columns method, grand_score, n_datasets, n_datasets_total, coverage, needs_labels, runtime_tier, worst_sec, env, output_kind. The score is the benchmark's own rule per dataset (overall="mean_overall": min-max scaled mean of per-metric max-ranks, averaged over the datasets the method was run on); datasets with fewer than min_methods methods are DROPPED (a lone method's min-max is 1.0 by construction) and a UserWarning summarises dropped datasets and partial coverage. modalities keeps methods consuming ALL of them (via find_methods); long_df scores your own frame (pd.concat([published, mine])) instead of loading; metrics overrides task. Raises ValueError when nothing can be ranked, FileNotFoundError when no stored results exist for the category / source.

docs.text:
mtb.list_methods(category: str | None = None, task: str | None = None, runnable: bool | None = None) -> list[str]

Return the registry method ids, optionally filtered to those declaring a given category and/or task.

docs.title: mtb.list_tasks
docs.text:
mtb.list_tasks() -> list[str]
# ['batch', 'classification', 'clustering', 'dimension_reduction', 'imputation', 'registration']

Return the sorted set of tasks declared across all method specs.

docs.title: mtb.find_methods
docs.text:
mtb.find_methods(category: str | None = None, task: str | None = None, needs_labels: bool | None = None,
                 atac: str | None = None, modalities: list[str] | set[str] | None = None,
                 runnable: bool | None = None, tunable: bool | None = None) -> list[str]

Return method ids matching every supplied filter. Every token is validated: a typo raises ValueError naming the valid vocabulary instead of silently matching nothing.

Parameters

  • category (str | None) - integration category the method must declare.
  • task (str | None) - one of list_tasks.
  • needs_labels (bool | None) - derived from the variants' roles: True means at least one variant takes a cell-type-label (cty) role as a REQUIRED input (method_info(m)["supports"][i]["needs_labels"] per variant).
  • atac (str | None) - exact match on the declared ATAC representation, "peak" or "gene_activity" (aliases "peaks" / "gas") - what the UPSTREAM script expects, which is not always what its role name suggests (moETM / scMM / iPOLNG take role atac_gas but consume peaks).
  • modalities (list[str] | set[str] | None) - keep methods that consume ALL of these base modality types (["rna", "atac"]); "protein" is accepted for adt and role tokens (atac_gas, rna1 ...) are reduced to their base type. Implicitly excludes stub methods without variants.
  • runnable (bool | None) - True: methods with at least one variant; False: only the stubs.
  • tunable (bool | None) - True: only methods exposing at least one hyperparameter on their command line.

docs.title: mtb.method_info
docs.text:
mtb.method_info(method: str, files_dir: Path | str | None = None, *, verbose: bool = False) -> dict

A flat dict combining the registry spec with the method's provenance. Keys: id, language, categories, tasks, env, atac, needs_labels (derived: any variant takes a cty role), status (verified = the command template was cross-checked against the upstream entrypoint and executed end to end on a reference dataset, recorded in notebooks/results/final_verification.tsv), setup_hint, variants (distinct upstream entrypoints), driver (package-side wrapper, or None), scripts_url, repo_url, version, reference ({doi, title, authors, journal, year} or None), notes (short summary), supports (per variant: category, modalities, output_kind, n_tunable, needs_labels), params (per variant: defaults, tunable, effective), fixed_in_script, upstream_knobs, upstream_url. env is the conda env run executes in - group_for - e.g. scmb_torch for SCALEX, scmb_cobolt3 for Cobolt. verbose=True adds notes_long (the upstream-knob audit prose); files_dir adds the catalog columns deep_learning and output.

docs.title: mtb.cite
docs.text:
mtb.cite(methods: list[str] | str | None = None, fmt: str = "bibtex") -> str

Citation text: the benchmark entry first, then one entry per method in the order given. methods=None -> the benchmark only; "all" -> every registry method; a list of ids (KeyError + hint on a typo). Methods whose DOI is not yet curated are emitted as a comment naming their repository, never silently dropped. fmt is "bibtex" (one @article per entry) or "text" (one "Authors. Title. Journal (year). https://doi.org/..." line each). Every DOI was resolved against Crossref.

docs.title: mtb.inputs_for
docs.text:
mtb.inputs_for(dataset: str, method: str, category: str, modalities: list[str] | set[str] | None = None,
               data_path: Path | str | None = None, check: bool | None = None) -> dict

Resolve a dataset folder + method to concrete {modality_role: path} input paths. The dataset tree is flat (<data_path>/<dataset>/<file>); each role is resolved to the file actually present - the role token or a known alias (atac_peak -> peak.h5, atac_gas -> atac.h5), falling back to <role>.h5. When modalities is omitted and the method has exactly one variant for the category, that variant is used; if several match, a ValueError lists the modality-sets and asks you to disambiguate. Use labels_for for the cell-type label files.

Parameters

  • dataset (str) - dataset folder name under data_path (e.g. "D28").
  • method (str) - registry method id.
  • category (str) - integration category (validated).
  • modalities (list[str] | set[str] | None) - exact modality-set to select a variant (protein accepted for adt).
  • data_path (Path | str | None) - override config.DEFAULT.data_path.
  • check (bool | None) - None (default): return best-effort paths but warn about missing ones; True: raise FileNotFoundError (listing what IS in the folder) and also run the content preflight - matrix orientation (ValueError for a cells x features file), label length (one row per cell of the modality it labels), and the data_dir content check - exactly what scan reports as files_ok / files_reason; False: silent.

docs.text:
mtb.labels_for(dataset: str, method: str | None = None, category: str | None = None, *,
               data_path: Path | str | None = None) -> dict

Return {name: path} of the cell-type label CSVs for a dataset - the *cty*.csv files in the (flat) dataset directory, under their dataset-specific names (cty.csv, rna_cty.csv, cty1.csv, ...), excluding tool-specific *_scjoint* reformats. Pass one of these paths to evaluate, e.g. labels=mtb.labels_for(ds)["cty"], or for a multi-file dataset list(labels_for(ds).values()) in batch order (a one-entry dict is accepted directly; a multi-entry dict raises with that hint). method / category are accepted so the call mirrors inputs_for and are ignored - labels are per dataset. mtb.data.fetch(*datasets: str, data_path=None, quiet: bool = False) -> Path

docs.title: mtb.plot.bubble
docs.text:
mtb.plot.bubble(long_df, *, metrics=None, methods=None, order=None, aggregate="dataset",
                cmap=None, title=None, save=None, show_language=True,
                require_complete=False, overall="rank") -> matplotlib.figure.Figure

Paper-style bubble table of a tidy long results frame: methods are rows (best first), metrics are columns grouped into the benchmark's task families, each family preceded by an Overall bar. A plain function - help(mtb.plot.bubble) shows this signature; mtb.plot.build_table(...) (numbers, a BubbleTable with methods, overall, matrix, raw, norm, ranks, blocks) and mtb.plot.render(table, cmap=, title=, show_language=) (figure) are the two halves.

Parameters

  • long_df (pd.DataFrame) - columns method, metric, value at least (what to_long, load_results and BatchResult.long return); dataset is needed for aggregate="summary". Concatenate frames to compare your method with the benchmark's.
  • metrics (list[str] | None) - metric codes to show, drawn in THIS order within each family block; alias tolerant; an unknown code raises ValueError naming the metrics present.
  • methods (list[str] | None) - methods to show (exact / canonical / case-insensitive); unknown -> ValueError with a hint.
  • order (list[str] | None) - row order for the listed methods; unlisted methods follow, best first. Only reorders, never filters; unknown names raise.
  • aggregate (str) - "dataset" (default; raw values, circles; several datasets are averaged per method with a UserWarning and dataset-tagged row labels) or "summary" (within-dataset max-ranks averaged over datasets, bars; a UserWarning lists methods missing from some datasets).
  • cmap (str | None) - colormap overriding the FIRST family's palette (default blues / greens / purples per family).
  • title (str | None), save (str | None) - figure title; fig.savefig(save, bbox_inches="tight"), format by suffix.
  • show_language (bool) - Py / R chip per row (? for methods not in the registry) and an L badge for label-consuming methods.
  • require_complete (bool) - with "summary": restrict to methods present in EVERY dataset (ValueError if none is).
  • overall (str) - "rank" (default: minmax(mean over metrics of max-rank(mean over datasets of within-dataset max-rank)), absence = rank 0) or "mean_overall" (mean over datasets of minmax(mean over metrics of within-dataset max-rank), absence skipped). Pass the same value to plot.bar for the same ordering; the formula in use is printed on the figure.

Raises ValueError for missing columns (with a hint when the frame looks like evaluate()'s wide output), unknown names, duplicate (method[, dataset], metric) rows (they would be silently averaged), bad aggregate / overall.

mtb.plot.bar(long_df, *, metrics=None, group: str | None = None, top: int | None = None,

docs.title: mtb.io.*
docs.text: The input-format adapter to and from the canonical scMultiBench .h5 (an HDF5 file with matrix/data of shape features x cells, plus matrix/features and matrix/barcodes; float64, gzip-compressed, chunked, like the shipped files).

docs.title: mtb.io.export_dataset
docs.text:
mtb.io.export_dataset(data, dataset_dir: Path | str, *, rna: str | None = "X", adt: str | None = None,
                      atac: str | None = None, atac_kind: str | None = None, labels: str | None = None,
                      batch: str | None = None, dtype: str = "float64", compression: str | None = "gzip") -> Path

Write an AnnData / MuData as a canonical benchmark dataset folder - rna.h5, adt.h5, atac_peak.h5 (+ a hard-linked atac.h5) or atac_gas.h5, and cty.csv - so that mtb.scan(name, data_path=dataset_dir.parent) and run_all work on your own data. Selectors: 'X', 'obsm:<key>', 'layer:<key>', 'mod:<name>' (MuData; optionally 'mod:<name>.obsm:<key>'); None skips the modality. atac_kind is required with atac: 'peak' (chr:start-end features) or 'gene_activity' (-> atac_gas.h5 only, so the gene-activity role never silently falls back to a peak matrix); a warning is raised when the feature names contradict the declared kind. labels is 'obs:<col>' (or 'mod:<name>.obs:<col>') -> cty.csv (header x); batch (same grammar) splits the cells per batch value and writes the numbered rna1.h5 / adt1.h5 / cty1.csv ... layout instead. All matrices are cells x features and written transposed; sparse matrices are streamed. Returns dataset_dir.

mtb.io.from_mudata(mdata, dataset_dir: Path | str, *, rna: str | None = "rna", adt: str | None = None,

                   batch: str | None = None, dtype: str = "float64", compression: str | None = "gzip") -> Path

docs.title: mtb.io.to_canonical
docs.text:
mtb.io.to_canonical(src, out: Path | str | None = None, modality: str | None = None, convert: bool = True, *,
                    layer: str | None = None, obsm: str | None = None, mod: str | None = None,
                    dtype: str = "float64", compression: str | None = "gzip", block: int = 1024) -> Path

Convert src to a canonical .h5 and return its path. src is an AnnData, a MuData (mod= required), or a path to .h5ad / .h5mu / .csv / .tsv (cells x features) / .loom / a canonical .h5 (passed through untouched). out is the output file, or an existing directory when modality is given - then the canonical filename (rna.h5, adt.h5, atac_peak.h5, atac_gas.h5, atac.h5) is appended. modality (rna | adt | atac | atac_peak | atac_gas; aliases protein, peak, gas / gene_activity) is validated, warns when ATAC feature names contradict the role, and with modality='adt' on an AnnData that has obsm keys requires obsm= / layer= to say where the protein matrix is. convert=False means "never write" (non-canonical input raises). Sparse matrices are streamed without densifying; dtype='float32' halves the uncompressed size.

docs.title: RunResult
docs.text:
mtb.run returns a RunResult dataclass. Its fields:

  • method (str) - the method id that was run.
  • out_dir (Path) - the working directory the command ran in.
  • cmd (list[str]) - the fully wrapped argv that was executed (incl. the conda run prefix).
  • output - the loaded primary output (e.g. the joint embedding ndarray; may be dims x cells - evaluate re-orients it).
  • extra (dict) - {file: loaded_output} for any declared extra outputs.
  • stdout (str) / stderr (str) - captured streams.

A failed run (non-zero exit) raises RuntimeError with the tail of stderr/stdout rather than returning a RunResult; a missing conda env raises EnvironmentError before anything is written.

docs.text:
If you use scMultiBench (or the multibench Python API) in your research, please cite the benchmark paper. When you run one of the wrapped integration methods, also cite that method's own publication.

TL;DR

Cite Liu, Ding et al., Nature Methods (2025) for the benchmark, and cite each integration method you actually run. mtb.cite([...]) prints both:

print(mtb.cite(["Matilda", "MOFA2"]))            # BibTeX: the benchmark + one entry per method
print(mtb.cite(res.summary.method, fmt="text"))  # every method a run_all sweep used
terminal
multibench cite Matilda MOFA2 --format bibtex --out refs.bib

Reproducibility

For methods reporting, mtb.run(...) returns a RunResult whose .cmd field is the exact command line that was executed, and run_all saves the per-method records under out_dir. docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
multibench is the Python API that wraps the scMultiBench benchmark (Liu, Ding et al., Nature Methods 2025). It is tested on Python 3.9+ on Linux and macOS - the API itself; the per-method conda environments are Linux-only. The package itself is lightweight, a handful of pure-Python data dependencies, so installing it takes under a minute with a warm cache.

TL;DR

conda create -n multibench python=3.11 -y && conda activate multibench
pip install multibench-sc
python -c "import multibench as mtb; print(mtb.__version__)"

Two layers, two install scopes

The multibench API only orchestrates the benchmark, it has light dependencies. The integration methods it runs each live in their own conda env (they have mutually incompatible deps). You install multibench once; you install a method's env only when you want to run that method. See Method environments below.

docs.title: Step 1, Create an isolated environment
docs.text:
Conda (recommended)Mamba (faster solver)venv terminal
conda create -n multibench python=3.11 -y
conda activate multibench
terminal
mamba create -n multibench python=3.11 -y
mamba activate multibench
terminal
python3.11 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

Why isolate?

Even though multibench's own footprint is small, a dedicated env keeps it cleanly separated from the per-method environments that the benchmark orchestrates via conda run. Conda is recommended because that orchestration relies on named conda envs.

docs.title: Step 2, Install multibench
docs.text:
Two ways in - both give you the same import multibench:

PyPI (your own data)Repository (tutorials) terminal
pip install multibench-sc

The full API in a 184 KB package: discovery, running methods (environments build from the shipped lockfiles; the method scripts fetch themselves on first run), evaluation and figures. Datasets and clones go to ~/.cache/multibench/.

terminal
git clone https://github.com/DSichang/scMultiBench.git
cd scMultiBench
pip install -e . --config-settings editable_mode=compat

What the tutorials use: also carries the stored benchmark tables their figure sections reproduce, and the notebooks themselves.

What multibench is

multibench is the Python API for the scMultiBench benchmark (imported throughout the docs as mtb). For the editable from source install, the compat editable mode writes a plain path entry so import multibench resolves from any working directory (not only the repo root). Plain pip install -e . works too, but the compat flag avoids an empty-namespace import surprise when you later call the API from a script outside the clone.

This pulls in the core data-handling stack and the evaluation stack:

Package Min version Used for numpy 1.24 array math, embeddings pandas 2.0 tidy metric frames, catalog tables h5py 3.8 canonical scMultiBench .h5 matrix I/O anndata 0.9 data container / format adapters matplotlib 3.7 scIB-style bubble plots pyyaml 6.0 method registry / config parsing scanpy / scib 1.9 / 1.1 the scIB metrics behind mtb.evaluate

What is not installed here

No deep-learning frameworks, no per-method packages (torch, scvi-tools, Seurat, etc.). Those belong to the individual method environments, not to multibench. Keeping the core thin is deliberate, you can load published results, plot, and resolve inputs without any heavy stack present.

docs.title: Step 3, Verify the install
docs.text:
terminal
python -c "import multibench as mtb; print(mtb.__version__)"

Expected output: the installed version string (e.g. 0.1.0). If a version prints, the public API is reachable. A quick smoke test of the read-only surface:

import multibench as mtb

print(mtb.list_tasks())                 # available tasks
print(mtb.list_methods(category="vertical"))   # methods declared for a category

docs.title: Method environments
docs.text:
This is the part that makes multibench different from an ordinary library. The benchmark wraps 40 integration methods across four categories (vertical, diagonal, mosaic, cross). Each method ships its own toolchain, totalVI needs scvi-tools, Seurat_v5 / Seurat_WNN / iNMF / Conos need R, scBridge / Portal / uniPort each pin their own PyTorch line, and these conflict with one another. There is no single env that can satisfy them all.

So multibench does not import a method's code. Instead, mtb.run(...):

  1. Resolves the method's command from the registry,
  2. Converts your inputs to the canonical scMultiBench .h5 (unless convert=False),
  3. Executes the command inside that method's own conda env via a cmd_template, default "conda run -n {env} {cmd}",
  4. Loads the typed output back into a RunResult.
import multibench as mtb

res = mtb.run(
    "SCALEX", category="diagonal", task="clustering",
    inputs={"rna": "data/D28/rna.h5", "atac_gas": "data/D28/atac_gas.h5"},   # mtb.data.fetch("D28") downloads it
    out_dir="runs/scalex_d28",
)
res.output    # the joint embedding (ndarray)
res.cmd       # the exact command that was executed (list[str])

Create the method's env first

mtb.run(...) preflights the env and raises EnvironmentError naming the install command if it does not exist; scan() reports the same per method in its env_ok column. Build it with multibench env install --methods <method> --packed --run (see below) before running. The method scripts themselves are never modified by multibench.

Custom orchestration

Not using conda envs by name? Override how the command is launched with cmd_template (e.g. a container wrapper), or point repo_path at a local checkout of the method scripts. The default is "conda run -n {env} {cmd}".

Every method in the registry is wired and run-verified: its command has been cross-checked against the real entrypoint and executed end-to-end on a reference dataset.

docs.title: Build the environments
docs.text:
The multibench package itself is ~2 MB; disk goes to the conda environments of the methods you choose to run. The repository commits one lockfile per environment, and the CLI builds them reproducibly (Linux; method environments are not supported on macOS). Install only what you need:

terminal
multibench env doctor                             # which envs exist / are missing
multibench env install --methods Matilda --run    # one method: its env only (2-14 GB)
multibench env install --category vertical --run  # one category (45-101 GB, see below)
multibench env install --run                      # the whole benchmark (29 envs, ~167 GB)

Add --packed to any env install to use prebuilt archives (download + unpack in minutes instead of a 10-30 minute solve-and-build). All 29 environments are covered: smaller archives ship as release assets, larger ones from Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.21928885, 10.5281/zenodo.21928889); if a download fails, the install falls back to the lockfile build automatically.

Measured per-category footprints: vertical ~101 GB (18 envs), diagonal ~58 GB (9), mosaic ~45 GB (7), cross ~71 GB (11) - categories share environments, so combinations cost less than their sum. env doctor is safe to run any time; env install skips environments that already exist, so it resumes after interruption.

docs.title: Get the data
docs.text:
The benchmark datasets are not part of the git clone, and for the tutorials you do not need to fetch anything by hand: each tutorial auto-downloads its own reference data (11-290 MB) from the repository's release assets into data/ on first run. Manual equivalent, e.g. for D11:

terminal
wget -qO- https://github.com/DSichang/scMultiBench/releases/download/data-v1/D11.tar.gz | tar xz -C data/

Available there: D11 (vertical, 11 MB), D28 (diagonal, 137 MB), D45 (mosaic, 290 MB), D46 (mosaic, 97 MB), D52 (cross, 179 MB). The full 65-dataset collection is linked from the scMultiBench README; unpack any of it under data/ at the repository root - mtb.config.DEFAULT.data_path defaults to exactly that folder, and every data_path= argument in the API accepts an alternative location.

docs.title: The evaluation stack
docs.text: mtb.evaluate(...) computes scIB metrics on a run output. Since v0.2, scib and scanpy install with the package - no extra step. (pip install -e ".[eval]" remains accepted for compatibility; it is now a no-op.)

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Stuck on install?

EnvironmentError: conda env '<env>' is not installed from mtb.run, or env_ok False in scan()

The method's conda env does not exist here. multibench env install --methods <method> --packed --run builds it (the message carries the exact command), or pass a custom cmd_template= to mtb.run(...) that launches the command another way.

ImportError: No module named scib when calling mtb.evaluate

scib and scanpy are dependencies since v0.2 and install with the package; this means multibench was installed with --no-deps or into a different interpreter. Re-run pip install multibench-sc (or pip install -e . in the clone) in the env you import from.

cLISI / iLISI / kBET come back as NaN

This is expected when the LISI binary or rpy2 is unavailable, it is a warning, not an error. Install the LISI binary / rpy2 to populate those rows; everything else still computes.

conda solver hangs for >2 minutes

Switch to mamba: conda install -n base -c conda-forge mamba then re-create the env with mamba. Or conda config --set solver libmamba to use libmamba globally.

unsupported input format from mtb.io.to_canonical

The adapter accepts .h5ad, .h5mu, .csv / .tsv, .loom, and in-memory AnnData / MuData. Convert other formats to one of these first, or pass an already-canonical scMultiBench .h5 (it is detected and passed through unchanged). For a whole dataset folder use mtb.io.export_dataset / multibench convert --rna ... --labels ....

Still broken?

Open an issue, paste the output of python -c "import multibench as mtb; print(mtb.__version__)" or your pip freeze.

docs.title: How scMultiBench works
docs.text:
scMultiBench is a systematic benchmark of single-cell multimodal omics integration methods, not a method itself. It categorises and evaluates 40 integration methods so you can pick the right one for your data.

(a–b) Multimodal single-cell technologies produce distinct data combinations, organised into four integration scenarios — vertical, diagonal, mosaic, and cross — by how the input data are structured. (c–d) Each scenario feeds seven downstream analytical tasks, each scored by its own evaluation-metric panel. (e) The 40+ integration methods and the scenarios, tasks, and modalities each one covers.

docs.title: What scMultiBench covers
docs.text:
The study organises integration into four scenarios, defined by how the input data are structured:

  • Vertical — one dataset with fully matched modalities (e.g. CITE-seq, 10x Multiome: RNA + ADT/ATAC from the same cells).
  • Diagonal — multiple datasets with non-overlapping modalities (e.g. scRNA-seq from one experiment, scATAC-seq from another - no shared cells).
  • Mosaic — multiple datasets with partially overlapping modalities, often joined by a bridge (e.g. an RNA-only batch, an ATAC-only batch, and one paired batch).
  • Cross — multiple datasets with matched modalities across batches (e.g. the same CITE-seq assay from several donors or sites).

Across these scenarios it benchmarks the 40 methods on seven downstream tasks: dimension reduction, batch correction, clustering, classification, feature selection, imputation, and spatial registration. The published benchmark spans 64 real and 22 simulated datasets (86 total) covering RNA, ADT (CITE-seq), ATAC, and spatial modalities.

docs.title: How it evaluates
docs.text:
Each task gets its own metric panel: scIB-style batch-correction and biological-conservation metrics (kBET, iLISI, ASW, graph connectivity, PCR, ARI, NMI, and more), classification accuracy and F1, marker overlap and correlation for feature selection, RMSE for imputation, and label-transfer and alignment scores for spatial registration, plus runtime and peak memory. Results are aggregated into per-method grand rank scores and distilled into a decision tree that recommends top methods per scenario and task (Fig. 6 of the paper; the interactive explorer carries the same rankings).

A key takeaway: no single method wins everywhere. Performance depends on the dataset, task, and metric, with a recurring trade-off between preserving biological signal and correcting batch effects.

docs.title: When to use scMultiBench
docs.text:
Use scMultiBench when you want to choose or compare integration methods for your own data:

  • Run any of 40+ methods through one typed API (multibench), each in its own environment.
  • Evaluate with scIB and task-specific metrics.
  • Explore rankings, bubble tables, and the interactive Shiny explorer.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
scMultiBench wraps the 40-method single-cell multimodal integration benchmark behind one clean Python surface, imported as multibench and aliased mtb by convention. This page walks the full loop in five steps: discover the methods that fit your data, plot the stored benchmark, run a method, evaluate that run, and plot your own result alongside the rest. Everything but step 3 runs on a laptop with pip install multibench-sc; step 3 needs the method's conda environment.

TL;DR

import multibench as mtb, pandas as pd

# 1. what can integrate unpaired RNA + ATAC (diagonal)?
mtb.find_methods(category="diagonal", modalities=["rna", "atac"])

# 2. plot the published diagonal benchmark for dataset D28
df = mtb.load_results("diagonal", dataset="D28")
mtb.plot.bubble(df, metrics=["ARI", "NMI", "ASW"], save="fig.pdf")

# 3. run a method on the fetchable D28 (needs the method's conda env)
mtb.data.fetch("D28")
res = mtb.run("SCALEX", "diagonal",
              inputs=mtb.inputs_for("D28", "SCALEX", "diagonal"),
              out_dir="/abs/path/out/scalex_d28")

# 4. score it with scIB metrics (labels in the embedding's cell order)
labels = mtb.labels_for("D28")
metrics = mtb.evaluate(res.output, task="clustering",
                       labels=[labels["rna_cty"], labels["atac_cty"]])

# 5. reshape and plot it next to the benchmark
mine = mtb.to_long(metrics, method="SCALEX_rerun", dataset="D28", category="diagonal")
mtb.plot.bubble(pd.concat([df, mine]), metrics=["ARI", "NMI", "ASW"])

docs.title: Step 1 - Discover methods for your data
docs.text:
The benchmark spans four integration categories - vertical (paired, same cells), diagonal (unpaired, bridged by features), mosaic (overlapping modalities with a bridge), and cross (fully-matched datasets). Start by filtering the registry down to the methods that consume your modalities.

import multibench as mtb

mtb.find_methods(category="diagonal", modalities=["rna", "atac"])
# -> ['SCALEX', 'Seurat_v5', 'VIPCCA', 'Portal', 'uniPort', 'sciCAN', 'scJoint', 'GLUE', ...]

find_methods accepts any combination of category, task, needs_labels, atac, modalities, runnable and tunable - every filter is ANDed, and a typo in any token raises ValueError naming the valid vocabulary. Once you have a candidate, inspect its spec and what it has been observed to cost:

info = mtb.method_info("SCALEX")
info["env"], info["atac"], info["needs_labels"], info["reference"]["doi"]
# ('scmb_torch', 'gene_activity', False, '10.1038/s41467-022-33758-z')
mtb.runtime_hint("SCALEX")
# {'tier': 'slow', 'worst_sec': 2233, 'observed': [{'dataset': 'D28', 'cells': 11014, 'sec': 2233}]}
mtb.recommend("diagonal", modalities=["rna", "atac"])   # ranked from the stored tables, with coverage

docs.title: Step 2 - Plot the stored results
docs.text:
Before running anything, you can reproduce the paper's scIB-style bubble tables straight from the shipped metric tables. load_results returns a tidy long frame (metric, value, method, dataset, category, clustering, source); plot.bubble turns it into a figure where each circle's radius tracks the method's rank and its fill tracks the metric value, with an Overall bar per metric family.

df = mtb.load_results("diagonal", dataset="D28")          # the paper's table, 14 methods
fig = mtb.plot.bubble(df, metrics=["ARI", "NMI", "ASW"], save="fig.pdf")

load_results also takes task, method, metric, clustering ("default", "louvain", or "kmeans") and source - "published" (the paper's numbers, default) or "rerun" (the package's own sweep, the tables behind the category tutorials). To rank methods across several datasets instead of within one, pass aggregate="summary" to plot.bubble, which averages each method's per-dataset ranks.

docs.title: Step 3 - Run a method
docs.text:
mtb.run builds the method's real command line, executes it in the method's own conda environment, and loads the typed output back into Python. inputs is a dict mapping each modality role to a file path; inputs_for resolves them for a benchmark dataset, and non-canonical inputs are auto-converted to the canonical scMultiBench .h5 first (pass convert=False to skip this). The method scripts themselves are never modified.

mtb.data.fetch("D28")                                      # 137 MB; no-op when present
res = mtb.run(
    method="SCALEX",
    category="diagonal",
    inputs=mtb.inputs_for("D28", "SCALEX", "diagonal"),    # {'rna': .../D28/rna.h5, 'atac_gas': .../D28/atac_gas.h5}
    out_dir="/abs/path/out/scalex_d28",
)

res.output      # the joint embedding, (11014, 10): 6,408 RNA + 4,606 ATAC cells x latent dims
res.cmd         # the exact argv that was executed
res.extra       # dict of any additional outputs
res.stdout      # captured stdout / stderr

The return value is a RunResult with fields method, out_dir, cmd, output, extra, stdout, and stderr.

Each method runs in its own conda env

run orchestrates per-tool environments via the default cmd_template="conda run -n {env} {cmd}", so the target env (for SCALEX, scmb_torch, from method_info(...)["env"]) must exist: multibench env install --methods SCALEX --packed --run builds it, and run raises EnvironmentError with that command when it is missing. To run inside the current interpreter instead, pass cmd_template="{cmd}". Use an absolute out_dir - the script runs with it as its working directory.

Your own data. mtb.run_all(dataset, category, out_dir=...) runs every method that fits a dataset folder and scores the outputs - the category tutorials are built on it. One call writes the folder from an AnnData:

mtb.io.export_dataset(adata, "data/MYCITE", rna="X", adt="obsm:protein", labels="obs:celltype")
mtb.scan("MYCITE", "vertical", data_path="data")     # files_ok / env_ok per method, with reasons
res = mtb.run_all("MYCITE", "vertical", data_path="data", out_dir="out/")
res.summary; res.plot()

docs.title: Step 4 - Evaluate your run
docs.text:
mtb.evaluate computes scIB metrics on a run output and returns a metric.csv-shaped frame (index = metric name, single "Value" column). Clustering metrics need the ground-truth cell-type labels; clustering is optional (omitted, scIB's optimal-resolution Leiden clustering is derived from the embedding). For task="batch" or task="all" you also pass batch labels - or a list of label files, one per batch.

labels = mtb.labels_for("D28")                   # {'atac_cty': ..., 'rna_cty': ...} - one file per modality
metrics = mtb.evaluate(
    res.output,
    task="clustering",
    labels=[labels["rna_cty"], labels["atac_cty"]],   # SCALEX stacks RNA cells, then ATAC cells
)
# index: ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1, cLISI   column: Value

labels can equally be a pandas.Series, an array, or an obs column name when output is an AnnData; only={"ARI", "NMI"} restricts the computation.

docs.title: Step 5 - Plot your own result
docs.text:
To compare your run against the benchmark, reshape evaluate's wide frame into the same long format load_results produces, then hand it to plot.bubble, concatenated with the stored frame from Step 2. Give your run a name of its own - the stored table already holds a SCALEX row, and duplicate (method, metric) rows raise rather than being silently averaged.

import pandas as pd

mine = mtb.to_long(metrics, method="SCALEX_rerun", dataset="D28", category="diagonal")

combined = pd.concat([df, mine], ignore_index=True)
mtb.plot.bubble(combined, metrics=["ARI", "NMI", "ASW"],
                title="D28: published table + our SCALEX re-run", save="compare.pdf")

Both frames are the same dataset, so the figure is a like-for-like comparison; a re-run does not reproduce the stored decimals exactly (methods are stochastic), so read ranks rather than digits - see Are my numbers comparable?. When you concatenate your dataset with a benchmark dataset instead, the comparison is cross-dataset: aggregate="dataset" then averages each method's values across the datasets it appears in (with a warning and dataset-tagged row labels), and aggregate="summary" ranks within each dataset first.

The same loop is available from the command line:

terminal
multibench plot bubble --category diagonal --dataset D28 \
    --metrics ARI,NMI,ASW --out fig.pdf
multibench evaluate --output out/scalex_d28/embedding.h5 --labels data/D28/rna_cty.csv \
    --method SCALEX_rerun --dataset D28 --category diagonal --out mine.csv

multibench also exposes list, find, scan, layout, convert, run, run-all, cite and env (doctor / plan / install) subcommands that mirror the Python API - multibench <command> --help documents every flag.

docs.text:
scMultiBench ships an interactive Shiny dashboard for exploring benchmark results in depth, scIB metric tables, integration/registration quality, feature-selection overlap, classification accuracy, and time/memory profiles, across every method and dataset, without writing any code.

Open the Shiny explorer ↗

The dashboard is an R Shiny app built on shinydashboard, plotly, and DT:

  "shiny", "shinydashboard", "dashboardthemes",

docs.title: What you can explore
docs.text:
• scIB metrics

    Batch-correction and bio-conservation sub-scores per method, summarised as the familiar scIB bubble tables and overall rankings.

  • Integration & registration

  • Feature selection

    Overlap and correlation of selected features across methods (intersection and rank-correlation views).

  • Classification

    Downstream cell-type classification accuracy built on each integrated embedding.

  • Time & memory

Modality roles and the filenames they resolve to:
    rna              rna.h5      - gene expression
    adt              adt.h5      - surface protein (CITE-seq antibody-derived tags)
    atac             atac.h5     - chromatin accessibility
    atac_gas         atac.h5     - ATAC as GENE-ACTIVITY scores  <-- note: plain atac.h5
    atac_peak        peak.h5     - ATAC as PEAKS                 <-- note: peak.h5, NOT atac.h5
    rna1/rna2/...    rna1.h5, rna2.h5, ... - one file per BATCH (mosaic/cross)
    adt1/adt2/...    adt1.h5, adt2.h5, ... - one file per BATCH (mosaic/cross)
    cty              cty.csv     - cell-type labels, ONE label set (vertical)
    rna_cty / atac_cty rna_cty.csv, atac_cty.csv - one label file PER MODALITY, used when RNA and ATAC come from different cells (diagonal)
    cty1/cty2/...    cty1.csv, cty2.csv, ... - one label file per BATCH (mosaic/cross)

!! ATAC: the role name does NOT guarantee the representation.
   atac_gas resolves to atac_gas.h5 if present, otherwise FALLS BACK
   to atac.h5 - and in the shipped multiome datasets (D12-D17) atac.h5
   contains PEAKS, not gene activity. Only D27/D28 ship a real
   atac_gas.h5. Verified by feature names: 12 atac.h5 files are peaks
   (chr1:3094772-3095489), 2 atac_gas.h5 files are gene activity.
   atac_peak resolves to atac_peak.h5, else peak.h5.
   This matters because methods disagree (lists from the registry;
   see mtb.find_methods(atac=...) / mtb.method_info(m)['atac']):
     need GENE ACTIVITY: SCALEX/scBridge/scMDC/Matilda/VIPCCA/Portal/uniPort/sciCAN/scJoint/UnitedNet/iNMF/online_iNMF/Conos
     need PEAKS:         Multigrate/Seurat_v5/MultiVI/Cobolt/scMVP/scMM/scMoMaT/moETM/MIRA/VIMCCA/SMILE/GLUE/MultiMAP/iPOLNG/StabMap/Seurat_v3/Seurat_WNN
   Feeding the wrong one runs to completion and returns a plausible
   but WRONG embedding - no error.
   Check what you actually have before trusting a cross-dataset result.
   scan() flags the commonest trap in its `caveat` column: an atac_gas
   role that fell back to an atac.h5 whose features are chr:start-end.

MODALITY FILE FORMAT (.h5) - easiest route first:
  mtb.io.to_canonical(src, dst)   converts an .h5ad and writes
  everything below correctly. Prefer it over building the file by hand.
  For a whole dataset in one call (every modality + labels, numbered
  per batch when batch= is given):
    mtb.io.export_dataset(adata, '<data_path>/MYDATA', rna='X',
                          adt='obsm:protein', labels='obs:cell_type')
  Both store matrix/data as float64, gzip-compressed and chunked, like
  the shipped files (a 3000x2000 8%-dense matrix is ~1.5 MB on disk).

  If you do build it yourself, ALL THREE datasets are required:
    matrix/data      the matrix, stored FEATURES x CELLS
    matrix/features  one entry per feature (row of matrix/data)
    matrix/barcodes  one entry per cell    (column of matrix/data)
  e.g. 2,000 genes x 5,000 cells -> matrix/data has shape (2000, 5000),
  matrix/features has 2000 entries and matrix/barcodes has 5000.
  NOTE this is the TRANSPOSE of the scanpy/AnnData convention
  (AnnData.X is cells x genes). scan() rejects a transposed file, and
  a file with only matrix/data fails with a KeyError about 'features'.
Labels are a single-column CSV: one header line (typically 'x'),
then one cell-type label per cell; the evaluator reads the first
column and skips the header.

SPATIAL REGISTRATION (task 'registration', category 'cross'):
  Methods: GPSA, PASTE, PASTE2, SPIRAL. They take a DIRECTORY of slices, not
  modality files - the role is `data_dir` and scan() shows modalities
  as '(data_dir)'; pass NO modalities to run_all/inputs_for.
    <data_path>/MYVISIUM/            (or <data_path>/MYVISIUM/processed/)
        slice_0.h5ad  slice_1.h5ad  ...   one AnnData per slice, >= 2
  Each .h5ad needs .X (expression, spots x genes) and
  .obsm['spatial'] (spot coordinates, spots x 2). The upstream
  scripts glob data_dir + '*.h5ad' WITHOUT sorting, so the slice
  index in the output follows glob order, not your numbering; SPIRAL
  also wants a UNIQUE leading token per filename (the part before
  the first '_') - the package stages symlinks for that when needed.
  Output: aligned_slice_<i>.h5ad per slice (coordinates, not an
  embedding), so run_all records RUN_OK_NO_EMBEDDING - clustering
  metrics do not apply, and registration metrics are NOT wired into
  mtb.evaluate in this version.
  scan() checks the dir for >= 2 .h5ad slices with obsm['spatial'].

cross: Several batches in which ALL modalities are present; the task is removing batch effects. (Spatial slice registration also lives here.)


ENVIRONMENTS
  Every method runs in its OWN conda env (they need mutually
  incompatible framework versions). scan() checks TWO gates per row -

Each modality file is HDF5 with three datasets:

dataset contents shape matrix/data the matrix, features x cells (n_features, n_cells) matrix/features one name per feature (n_features,) matrix/barcodes one id per cell (n_cells,)

That is the transpose of the AnnData convention (AnnData.X is cells x genes); the mtb.io writers below handle it, and scan() rejects a transposed file at preflight rather than letting a method fail half an hour in. The label CSV is a single column with one header line (typically x) and one label per cell, in the same order as matrix/barcodes of the matching modality file. For ATAC, check which representation a method wants - gene-activity scores or peaks - because the wrong one runs to completion and returns a plausible but wrong embedding. Now a real dataset the package has never seen: a 60% cell subsample of D52 under a new name, built with ordinary h5py/pandas code so the per-file rule (matching files keep the same cell index) is visible.

import os, shutil
import h5py
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def subsample_dataset(src_dir, dst_dir, frac=0.6, seed=0):
    """Copy a dataset to a new name, keeping a random fraction of the cells.

    Files sharing a cell count get the SAME kept-cell index, so modality files
    and their label CSVs stay aligned - which is exactly the property your own
    export pipeline must preserve. The output is the canonical layout:
    matrix/data as features x cells, plus matrix/features and matrix/barcodes.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    os.makedirs(dst_dir, exist_ok=True)
    counts, keep = {}, {}
    for fn in sorted(os.listdir(src_dir)):
        p = os.path.join(src_dir, fn)
        if fn.endswith(".h5"):
            with h5py.File(p) as f:
                if "matrix/data" in f:
                    counts[fn] = f["matrix/data"].shape[1]   # features x cells
        elif fn.endswith(".csv"):
            counts[fn] = len(pd.read_csv(p))
    for n in set(counts.values()):
        k = max(50, int(n * frac))
        keep[n] = np.sort(rng.choice(n, size=k, replace=False))
    for fn, n in counts.items():
        sp, dp = os.path.join(src_dir, fn), os.path.join(dst_dir, fn)
        idx = keep[n]
        if fn.endswith(".csv"):
            pd.read_csv(sp).iloc[idx].to_csv(dp, index=False)
        else:
            with h5py.File(sp) as f, h5py.File(dp, "w") as g:
                grp = g.create_group("matrix")
                grp.create_dataset("data", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/data"])[:, idx])
                if "matrix/features" in f:
                    grp.create_dataset("features", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/features"]))
                if "matrix/barcodes" in f:
                    grp.create_dataset("barcodes", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/barcodes"])[idx])
    return dst_dir

docs.title: Cross integration¶
docs.text:
Cross integration has several batches in which all modalities are present; the task is removing batch effects while keeping biological structure. Spatial registration (PASTE, PASTE2, SPIRAL, GPSA) also lives under cross - see the note at the end.

Reference dataset: D52 (23,478 cells). The stored results shipped with these notebooks were produced on it, so every table here reproduces.

docs.title: 1. Install¶
docs.text: Two layers: the multibench package (~2 MB) and the conda environments of the methods you run. On Colab, run the first cell and let the kernel restart once - then keep running from the next cell. Sections 2-3 (running methods) need the environments and a Linux runtime with the disk for them; sections 4-5 (stored results, reference) need only the package.

docs.title: 2. Run the analysis¶
docs.text: One call is the whole pipeline: resolve each method's inputs, run it in its own conda env, load the embeddings, score them with scIB metrics. Here UINMF, sciPENN, StabMap. StabMap is among the fastest cross methods - run_sec in the summary is the measured time on our host.

docs.title: 3. Your own data¶
docs.text: The same three calls - scan, run_all, plot - on a folder the package has never seen. A dataset is a folder of flat files named by category:

docs.title: 4. Reading stored results¶
docs.text: Section 2 ran three methods; the package ships the full sweep for D52 - every wired method at default settings, hours of compute - so the paper's figures reproduce from stored results in seconds. load_results reads them back as the tidy frame mtb.plot.bubble takes; source="rerun" selects the package's own re-execution (the tables behind this notebook), "published" the paper's tables, and every row says which it came from in its source column.

docs.title: What runs on a dataset, and why not¶
docs.text: scan inspects a folder and reports every runnable method - and for the rest, the exact reason (missing file, missing environment, wrong layout). Nothing executes.

docs.title: What each method exposes for tuning¶
docs.text: method_info(m)["supports"] lists a method's variants with how many hyperparameters each exposes on its command line; mtb.params_for(m, CATEGORY, modalities) names them. An empty tunable is honest: many upstream scripts hardcode their hyperparameters, and this package never edits upstream code.

docs.title: What the registry knows about a method, and how to cite it¶
docs.text: method_info carries the upstream reference, repository and version next to the run metadata (verbose=True adds the long audit notes); mtb.cite emits the benchmark entry plus one per method you ran.

docs.title: The metrics¶
docs.text:
Two families, matching the paper's grouping. All are higher = better, on [0, 1] except ARI (slightly negative at chance level).

family metrics what they measure clustering / bio-conservation ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1, cLISI does the embedding separate the annotated cell types? batch correction ASW_batch, GC, iLISI (+ opt-in kBET) are the batches mixed within each cell type?

Batch metrics appear only when the dataset has real batches - their absence on a single-batch dataset is correct, not missing data. kBET is opt-in (mtb.evaluate(..., slow_metrics=True)) because it is much slower than the rest.

docs.title: Coverage of the paper¶
docs.text: scan() answers "what runs on this dataset"; this answers how many of the methods the paper benchmarks for cross the package wires at all.

docs.title: Troubleshooting¶
docs.text: symptom meaning fix files_ok False: input files not found a required file is absent the reason names the exact file and lists what IS in the folder env_ok False that method's conda env is not built the reason carries the one-method multibench env install ... command ... looks like cells x features matrix stored transposed re-export with mtb.io.to_canonical / export_dataset a method FAILs in seconds wrong input representation or layout read res.failures.iloc[0]["error"] - the full command line and stderr tail are there a method TIMEOUTs slow, not broken raise timeout=; runtime tiers in scan are measured, not guessed label_order_confidence low several label files fit the cell count check label_order_candidates in the record batch metrics scored against the wrong batches batch_source="file_of_origin" is the label-file rule res.rescore(batch=my_vector) re-scores the stored outputs without re-running

docs.title: Spatial registration¶
docs.text: PASTE, PASTE2, SPIRAL and GPSA are cross-integration methods whose output is aligned spatial coordinates, not an embedding - their status reports RUN_OK_NO_EMBEDDING and clustering metrics genuinely do not apply. They take a directory of per-slice .h5ad files (.X + obsm['spatial']); the SPATIAL REGISTRATION block of describe_layout("cross") above is the contract, and scan checks the directory for it.

import os, shutil
import h5py
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def subsample_dataset(src_dir, dst_dir, frac=0.6, seed=0):
    """Copy a dataset to a new name, keeping a random fraction of the cells.

    Files sharing a cell count get the SAME kept-cell index, so modality files
    and their label CSVs stay aligned - which is exactly the property your own
    export pipeline must preserve. The output is the canonical layout:
    matrix/data as features x cells, plus matrix/features and matrix/barcodes.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    os.makedirs(dst_dir, exist_ok=True)
    counts, keep = {}, {}
    for fn in sorted(os.listdir(src_dir)):
        p = os.path.join(src_dir, fn)
        if fn.endswith(".h5"):
            with h5py.File(p) as f:
                if "matrix/data" in f:
                    counts[fn] = f["matrix/data"].shape[1]   # features x cells
        elif fn.endswith(".csv"):
            counts[fn] = len(pd.read_csv(p))
    for n in set(counts.values()):
        k = max(50, int(n * frac))
        keep[n] = np.sort(rng.choice(n, size=k, replace=False))
    for fn, n in counts.items():
        sp, dp = os.path.join(src_dir, fn), os.path.join(dst_dir, fn)
        idx = keep[n]
        if fn.endswith(".csv"):
            pd.read_csv(sp).iloc[idx].to_csv(dp, index=False)
        else:
            with h5py.File(sp) as f, h5py.File(dp, "w") as g:
                grp = g.create_group("matrix")
                grp.create_dataset("data", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/data"])[:, idx])
                if "matrix/features" in f:
                    grp.create_dataset("features", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/features"]))
                if "matrix/barcodes" in f:
                    grp.create_dataset("barcodes", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/barcodes"])[idx])
    return dst_dir

docs.title: Diagonal integration¶
docs.text:
Diagonal integration is the hard case: RNA and ATAC come from different cells, with no pairing and no shared cell ids, so a method must align two populations through a shared feature space (for RNA + ATAC, gene-activity scores, computed upstream of this package by e.g. Signac or ArchR). If your RNA and ATAC come from the SAME cells (10x multiome), that is vertical integration - use that tutorial instead.

Reference dataset: D28 (6,408 RNA + 4,606 ATAC cells). The stored results shipped with these notebooks were produced on it, so every table here reproduces.

docs.title: 1. Install¶
docs.text: Two layers: the multibench package (~2 MB) and the conda environments of the methods you run. On Colab, run the first cell and let the kernel restart once - then keep running from the next cell. Sections 2-3 (running methods) need the environments and a Linux runtime with the disk for them; sections 4-5 (stored results, reference) need only the package.

docs.title: 2. Run the analysis¶
docs.text: One call is the whole pipeline: resolve each method's inputs, run it in its own conda env, load the embeddings, score them with scIB metrics. Here online_iNMF, iNMF, scJoint. online_iNMF is among the fastest methods here - run_sec in the summary is the measured time on our host.

docs.title: 3. Your own data¶
docs.text: The same three calls - scan, run_all, plot - on a folder the package has never seen. A dataset is a folder of flat files named by category:

docs.title: 4. Reading stored results¶
docs.text: Section 2 ran three methods; the package ships the full sweep for D28 - every wired method at default settings, hours of compute - so the paper's figures reproduce from stored results in seconds. load_results reads them back as the tidy frame mtb.plot.bubble takes; source="rerun" selects the package's own re-execution (the tables behind this notebook), "published" the paper's tables, and every row says which it came from in its source column.

docs.title: What runs on a dataset, and why not¶
docs.text: scan inspects a folder and reports every runnable method - and for the rest, the exact reason (missing file, missing environment, wrong layout). Nothing executes.

docs.title: What each method exposes for tuning¶
docs.text: method_info(m)["supports"] lists a method's variants with how many hyperparameters each exposes on its command line; mtb.params_for(m, CATEGORY, modalities) names them. An empty tunable is honest: many upstream scripts hardcode their hyperparameters, and this package never edits upstream code.

docs.title: What the registry knows about a method, and how to cite it¶
docs.text: method_info carries the upstream reference, repository and version next to the run metadata (verbose=True adds the long audit notes); mtb.cite emits the benchmark entry plus one per method you ran.

docs.title: The metrics¶
docs.text:
Two families, matching the paper's grouping. All are higher = better, on [0, 1] except ARI (slightly negative at chance level).

family metrics what they measure clustering / bio-conservation ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1, cLISI does the embedding separate the annotated cell types? batch correction ASW_batch, GC, iLISI (+ opt-in kBET) are the batches mixed within each cell type?

Batch metrics appear only when the dataset has real batches - their absence on a single-batch dataset is correct, not missing data. kBET is opt-in (mtb.evaluate(..., slow_metrics=True)) because it is much slower than the rest.

docs.title: Coverage of the paper¶
docs.text: scan() answers "what runs on this dataset"; this answers how many of the methods the paper benchmarks for diagonal the package wires at all.
