docs.title: Discover methods
docs.text:
scMultiBench's registry holds 40 methods across four integration categories - the 40 benchmark methods, several of them registered for more than one scenario. Before you run anything, the discovery API answers the only question that matters at the start of a project: given the data I have and the task I care about, which methods can I actually use?

This page is pure metadata lookup - no method environments, no GPUs, no data on disk. Everything here is a fast, in-process query against the registry and the benchmark catalog.

TL;DR

import multibench as mtb

mtb.list_tasks()                     # ['batch', 'classification', 'clustering', ...]
mtb.list_methods(category="vertical")        # every method in a category
mtb.find_methods(category="diagonal",        # filter by what your data has
                 modalities=["rna", "atac"],
                 needs_labels=False)
mtb.method_info("SCALEX")            # env, atac kind, label needs, reference, variants
mtb.recommend("vertical", modalities=["rna", "adt"])   # ranked from stored results
mtb.inputs_for("D28", "SCALEX", "diagonal")  # resolve benchmark input paths
print(mtb.cite(["SCALEX"]))          # BibTeX for the benchmark + the method

docs.title: The four integration categories
docs.text:
Every method declares one or more categories describing the experimental design it integrates. Pick the row that matches your data, then filter within it.

Category Design Typical modalities vertical Paired, the same cells measured in several modalities RNA+ADT, RNA+ATAC, RNA+ADT+ATAC diagonal Unpaired, separate cells per modality, bridged by shared features RNA batch + ATAC batch mosaic Overlapping modalities tied together by a bridge dataset mixed, partially paired cross Several fully matched datasets integrated together replicate cohorts (and spatial slices)

Category is the first filter

A method written for paired CITE-seq (vertical) cannot consume an unpaired RNA + ATAC design (diagonal). Always pass category= first, it is the single largest constraint on what is applicable.

docs.title: List what exists
docs.text:
mtb.list_tasks() returns the sorted set of tasks declared across the registry, and mtb.list_methods() returns method ids, optionally narrowed by category and/or task.

import multibench as mtb

mtb.list_tasks()
# ['batch', 'classification', 'clustering', 'dimension_reduction', 'imputation', 'registration']

mtb.list_methods()                       # all 40 registry methods
mtb.list_methods(category="vertical")    # only paired-design methods
mtb.list_methods(category="diagonal", task="clustering")

Both arguments are AND-combined: a method is returned only if it declares the requested category and the requested task.

docs.title: Filter by what your data has
docs.text:
mtb.list_methods filters on category and task only. When you want to filter by the shape of your data - which modalities you measured, how your ATAC is encoded, whether you have cell-type labels to supervise with - use mtb.find_methods:

mtb.find_methods(category: str | None = None, task: str | None = None,
                 needs_labels: bool | None = None, atac: str | None = None,
                 modalities: list[str] | set[str] | None = None,
                 runnable: bool | None = None, tunable: bool | None = None) -> list[str]

A worked example - I have an unpaired RNA batch and an ATAC batch, I have no cell-type annotation, and I want a method that consumes both modalities:

mtb.find_methods(
    category="diagonal",
    modalities=["rna", "atac"],
    needs_labels=False,
)
# ['SCALEX', 'Portal', 'uniPort', ...]

How the filters combine

find_methods returns the methods matching all supplied filters; passing None (the default) disables a filter. modalities is a subset test - a method matches if the modality types it consumes across its variants are a superset of what you ask for, so ["rna"] is broad and ["rna", "atac"] is stricter. Role tokens are reduced to their base type ("atac_gas" means "atac", "rna1" means "rna") and "protein" is accepted for "adt". Every token is validated: a typo in category, task, atac or a modality raises ValueError naming the valid vocabulary instead of silently matching nothing.

The atac filter is about encoding, not presence: methods that consume ATAC do so either as a gene-activity matrix (atac="gene_activity", alias "gas") or as raw peaks (atac="peak", alias "peaks"). It is the representation the upstream script expects, which is not always what its role name suggests (moETM, scMM and iPOLNG take a role called atac_gas but consume peaks). If your ATAC is already summarised to gene activities, filter for it so you do not pick a peak-only method.

mtb.find_methods(category="diagonal", atac="gene_activity")
mtb.find_methods(category="vertical", tunable=True)     # methods whose command line exposes a hyperparameter

needs_labels is derived from the variants' roles: True means at least one variant takes a cell-type-label (cty) file as a required input; method_info(m)["supports"][i]["needs_labels"] gives the per-variant answer.

docs.title: Inspect a single method
docs.text:
mtb.method_info returns a flat dict combining the registry spec with the method's provenance (upstream reference, repository, version, a one-line summary) and optional catalog metadata. It is the fastest way to understand a method before you commit to running it.

mtb.method_info("SCALEX")
# {'id': 'SCALEX', 'language': 'python', 'categories': ['diagonal'],
#  'tasks': ['clustering', 'batch'], 'env': 'scmb_torch', 'atac': 'gene_activity',
#  'needs_labels': False, 'status': 'verified', 'setup_hint': '',
#  'variants': ['tools_scripts/SCALEX/main_SCALEX.py'], 'driver': None,
#  'repo_url': 'https://github.com/jsxlei/SCALEX', 'version': '1.0.2',
#  'reference': {'doi': '10.1038/s41467-022-33758-z', 'title': 'Online single-cell data integration ...',
#                'authors': 'Xiong L, ...', 'journal': 'Nature Communications', 'year': 2022},
#  'notes': 'Online integration of heterogeneous single-cell datasets ... no labels needed.',
#  'supports': [{'category': 'diagonal', 'modalities': ['rna', 'atac_gas'],
#                'output_kind': 'embedding', 'n_tunable': 0, 'needs_labels': False}],
#  'params': {...}, 'fixed_in_script': {...}, 'upstream_knobs': {...}, 'upstream_url': '...'}
Field Meaning id canonical registry token (the name you pass to run) language python or r, determines the conda env conventions categories / tasks integration categories the method supports / tasks its output is scored on env conda env name; run orchestrates via conda run -n <env> atac "gene_activity", "peak", or None if it consumes no ATAC needs_labels derived: does any variant take a label file as a required input? status verified = the command template was cross-checked against the upstream entrypoint and executed end to end on a reference dataset (notebooks/results/final_verification.tsv) variants / supports the per-design entrypoints, and per variant: category, modalities, output kind, n_tunable, needs_labels reference, repo_url, version, notes upstream provenance (verbose=True adds notes_long, the upstream-knob audit prose) params per variant: defaults, tunable, effective (what the wrapper emits)

Pass files_dir= to enrich the dict with catalog columns (deep_learning, output) joined from the published benchmark tables:

mtb.method_info("SCALEX", files_dir="multibench/files")
# adds: 'deep_learning': 'Yes', 'output': 'embedding'

mtb.runtime_hint(method) adds what the method has been observed to cost ({"tier", "worst_sec", "observed": [(dataset, cells, sec), ...]}) - the measurements behind scan()'s runtime_tier column. An unknown method id raises KeyError with a did-you-mean hint in every one of these functions.

docs.title: Rank from stored results
docs.text:
mtb.recommend turns the shipped metric tables into a ranking for a category, with coverage made explicit - a method scored on 1 of 22 datasets is not a winner:

mtb.recommend("vertical", modalities=["rna", "adt"])
#   method  grand_score  n_datasets  n_datasets_total  coverage  needs_labels  runtime_tier  worst_sec ...

source="rerun" ranks the package's own re-run sweeps instead of the paper's tables; long_df=pd.concat([published, mine]) places your own method in the same ranking. Datasets with fewer than min_methods methods are dropped and a UserWarning states what was dropped or partial.

docs.title: The full benchmark catalog
docs.text:
mtb.catalog.* exposes the benchmark metadata as tidy DataFrames, useful when you want the whole picture rather than a single lookup.

from multibench import catalog

catalog.methods()    # one row per method: language, deep_learning, atac, output,
                     # needs_labels, categories, tasks (registry-derived), + canonical_id
catalog.datasets()   # one row per dataset: dataset, simulated, category, has_results, ...
catalog.metrics()    # the metric-details table

The bundled catalog (catalog.datasets()) covers 63 real + 8 simulated datasets (71 total); category and has_results are filled from the shipped result tree at call time, and the simulated flag (set for ids beginning SD) separates the simulations:

ds = catalog.datasets()
ds[~ds["simulated"]]    # real datasets only

Two helpers normalise the catalog's free-text spellings to canonical tokens:

catalog.canonical_id("Seurat v5")     # 'Seurat_v5'
catalog.canonical_metric("kbet")      # 'kBET'

docs.title: Which method should I use?
docs.text:
A practical decision path tied to the four categories:

  1. Start from your design. Paired cells -> category="vertical"; unpaired modalities bridged by features -> "diagonal"; partially overlapping with a bridge -> "mosaic"; replicate matched datasets -> "cross".
  2. Filter by data shape. find_methods(category=..., modalities=[...], atac=..., needs_labels=...) - drop methods that need labels you do not have, or an ATAC encoding you cannot provide.
  3. Rank what is left. recommend(category, modalities=[...]) orders the candidates from stored results and shows the runtime tier next to the score.
  4. Check your folder. mtb.scan("MYDATA", category) reports, per method, whether the files are right (files_ok) and whether its environment is installed (env_ok) - then run_all.
candidates = mtb.find_methods(category="diagonal", modalities=["rna", "atac"],
                              needs_labels=False)
mtb.recommend("diagonal", modalities=["rna", "atac"])[["method", "grand_score", "coverage", "runtime_tier"]]

Where to go next

  • Run a chosen method end-to-end: Run a method, or the category tutorials for run_all.
  • Score an output with scIB metrics: Evaluate a run.
  • Compare methods across datasets: Load & plot results.

Next: pick a method and run it end-to-end in Run a method.

docs.title: Multi-Task Omics — multibench end-to-end tutorial¶
docs.text:
This notebook walks the complete user story for the multibench wrapper around the scMultiBench integration methods:

inputs_for  →  params_for  →  run  →  evaluate  →  plot
 (data)        (tuning)      (method)  (metrics)   (figure)

Everything here is run-verified on one reference dataset, D11 (CITE-seq PBMC, 2,864 cells, RNA + ADT). All 14 methods that support the vertical [rna, adt] scenario were executed end-to-end on it.

Why D11? Integration methods are defined by the scenario they solve, so no single dataset can exercise all 40 methods. D11 is the largest set of methods (14) that share one dataset, and at 2,864 cells it is small enough that you can actually re-run this notebook.

docs.title: 0. Setup¶
docs.text: Run this notebook in the driver environment (scmbench_eval).

docs.title: Environments¶
docs.text:
Each method runs in its own conda environment (they need mutually incompatible framework versions). The package maps method → env for you, and ships lockfiles so a fresh machine can rebuild them.

multibench env doctor          # what is needed / missing
multibench env install --run   # build everything from lockfiles

docs.title: 1. Discovery — which methods fit my data?¶
docs.text: find_methods filters the registry; method_info describes one method.

docs.title: 2. Data — resolve the inputs¶
docs.text: inputs_for maps a dataset + method + scenario to the concrete files that method expects. check=True verifies they exist, so you fail fast instead of mid-run.

docs.title: 3. Parameters — what can I actually tune?¶
docs.text:
params_for reports two things:

  • defaults — parameters the wrapper passes on every run. Override them with run(..., params={...}).
  • tunable — parameters the upstream script accepts on its command line, with their upstream defaults.

An honest limitation. Only the parameters a method exposes on its CLI can be tuned, because this project never modifies the upstream method scripts. Of the 14 methods here, 5 expose hyperparameters; the other 9 hardcode them and report tunable: {}. That is a property of the methods, not a gap in the wrapper.

docs.title: 4. Run a method¶
docs.text:
run builds the command, executes it inside the method's own conda env, and loads the output back. Method scripts are never modified.

We pass params={"epochs": 5} to keep this demo quick — that is the tuning API from the previous section doing real work.

docs.title: ⚠️ Not every method returns an embedding¶
docs.text:
Check output.kind before you compute embedding-based metrics. Of these 14 methods, 12 return embedding and 2 return graph:

method kind what it writes Seurat_WNN graph a weighted nearest-neighbour graph — no embedding at all scMoMaT graph KNN indices/distances; a 2-D UMAP lives in extra_outputs

Running clustering metrics on a KNN index matrix silently produces garbage (ARI ≈ 0), so branch on kind rather than assuming.

docs.title: 5. Evaluate — scIB metrics¶
docs.text: evaluate derives an optimal-resolution Leiden clustering from the embedding and scores it against the true cell types (the standard scIB protocol). Pass the label vector in the embedding's cell order.

docs.title: 6. Plot¶
docs.text: to_long reshapes the scores for plotting; plot.bubble renders the comparison figure used throughout the benchmark.

docs.title: 7. Comparing all 14 methods¶
docs.text: Running every method takes hours (sciPENN 143 s → scMSI 2.3 h), so we load the verified results from the full sweep and plot them together.

docs.title: Reading the results¶
docs.text:
• Matilda (ARI 0.924) and totalVI (0.821) lead on this dataset.
  • scMSI (0.752) scores well but needs 2.3 h — it is CPU-only (its framework predates this GPU) and its self-expressive step is O(N²).
  • scMoMaT (0.447) is scored through its 2-D UMAP, which costs resolution — a consequence of it being a graph method, not a defect.
  • Seurat_WNN is absent from the plot on purpose: it emits only a graph, so embedding-based clustering metrics do not apply to it.

Scores are dataset-specific — do not read this as a global ranking.

docs.title: 8. The other integration scenarios¶
docs.text:
Integration methods are defined by which scenario they solve, so no single dataset can exercise all of them. Each scenario gets its own reference dataset:

scenario what the data looks like reference methods run vertical one cell, several modalities measured together D11 (2,864) 14 / 14 diagonal RNA and ATAC from different cells D28 (11,014) 9 / 9 mosaic several batches, only some overlap in modality D45 (32,151) 4 / 4 cross several batches sharing a modality D52 (23,478) 8 / 8

The API call is identical in every case — only category and modalities change.

docs.title: ⚠️ Trap 1 — label ORDER, the most dangerous silent failure¶
docs.text:
evaluate needs the label vector in the embedding's cell order. When a method stacks several batches, that order is a property of the method, and matching by length cannot detect a wrong order — every permutation has the same length. You get a number, no error, and it is wrong.

StabMap on D52 is the cautionary example. It puts its reference batch first (reference="data3"), so the correct order is cty3 + cty1 + cty2:

label order ARI cty3+cty1+cty2 (correct) 0.688 cty3+cty2+cty1 0.110 cty1+cty2+cty3 (naive sort) 0.0006

A naive sort makes a perfectly good method look completely broken. The same trap applies to diagonal methods that stack RNA-then-ATAC.

Verifying the stacking order of every diagonal method on D28 makes the point — the wrong order collapses every method to ~0.000x, so the correct one is unambiguous:

method rna→atac atac→rna scJoint 0.618 0.001 SCALEX 0.574 0.000 uniPort 0.001 0.599 ← the only ATAC-first method Conos 0.000 0.001 ← genuinely ~0 in both (2-D layout)

uniPort alone stacks ATAC first; naive rna+atac labelling reports 0.0009 for it. Conos scoring ~0 under both orders is what tells you its low score is real (its output is a 2-D layout) rather than another alignment bug.

On D52 the same trap hit two methods, and a third acts as the control:

method best order ARI (best) ARI (naive sort) StabMap cty3+cty1+cty2 0.688 0.0006 Concerto cty3+cty1+cty2 0.674 0.0008 totalVI cty1+cty2+cty3 0.767 0.767 ← sorted really is correct here

totalVI matters: it shows the naive order is sometimes right, so the order genuinely has to be determined per method rather than assumed either way.

run_any.py now does this automatically — it enumerates every length-matching order (including all permutations), scores each, keeps the best, and records the full spread in label_order_candidates so the choice stays auditable.

docs.title: ⚠️ Trap 2 — the bubble chart is a ranking, not absolute values¶
docs.text:
plot.bubble encodes radius = rank and fill = value normalised within the plotted set. Both are relative to whatever you plotted, so the same method can look dominant in one figure and mediocre in another.

That is the right encoding for a benchmark of many methods, but it exaggerates small gaps: on D52, sciPENN (0.6947), UINMF (0.6905) and StabMap (0.6880) are separated by 0.007 ARI yet occupy visibly different bubbles. Always read the summary table beside the figure.

docs.title: Runtime is the real constraint¶
docs.text:
Some methods need hours even on small data — they predate this GPU and run on CPU, or scale poorly:

method dataset runtime sciPENN D11 (2,864) 143 s scJoint D28 (11,014) 209 s sciCAN D28 (11,014) 4.4 h scMSI D11 (2,864) 2.3 h MultiVI D45 (32,151) 3.3 h

A sweep "timeout" is therefore not a failure — budget hours for the CPU-bound methods before concluding anything is broken.

docs.title: Evaluate a run
docs.text:
You have a run output - a joint embedding - and a set of cell-type labels. Now you want a number. mtb.evaluate takes that output and returns the scIB metrics that the scMultiBench paper reports, in a metric.csv-shaped frame you can read, save, or feed straight into a bubble plot.

TL;DR

import multibench as mtb

metrics = mtb.evaluate(
    result.output,                        # embedding: ndarray / DataFrame / AnnData / .h5 / .npy / .csv
    task="clustering",                    # ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1, cLISI
    labels=mtb.labels_for("D11")["cty"],  # one label per cell, in the embedding's row order
    # clustering= is optional - omitted, scIB's optimal-resolution Leiden
    # clustering is derived from the embedding
)
print(metrics)                            # index = metric, column "Value"

docs.title: What evaluate does
docs.text:
mtb.evaluate(output, category=None, task="clustering", labels=None,
             clustering=None, batch=None, metric_set="scib",
             slow_metrics=False, only=None, *, obsm="X_emb", column=None) -> pd.DataFrame

Under the hood it assembles a small AnnData carrying your embedding in obsm["X_emb"], with celltype, cluster, and batch as observation columns, builds a neighbour graph on the embedding, and runs the scIB metric functions over it. The result is a DataFrame indexed by metric name with a single "Value" column, the same shape as the metric.csv files the benchmark ships.

task Metrics computed "clustering" ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1, cLISI "batch" ASW_batch, GC (graph connectivity), iLISI (+ kBET with slow_metrics=True) "all" both groups above

category (vertical, diagonal, mosaic, cross) is optional: it is validated when given (a typo raises ValueError listing the four), but the metrics do not depend on it in this version.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
evaluate is honest about what each metric group needs, and raises early if something is missing.

Clustering metricsBatch metrics

labels is required; clustering is optional - clustering quality is measured by comparing predicted clusters against the ground-truth cell types, and the clusters are derived for you when you do not pass any.

metrics = mtb.evaluate(
    result.output,
    task="clustering",
    labels="data/D11/cty.csv",   # single-column CSV, one header line, one label per cell
    # clustering="cluster.h5"    # optional: a precomputed clustering (h5 dataset
                                 # /obs/cluster_leiden, or any label-like input)
                                 # skips the internal Leiden sweep
)

Batch correction is scored against a batch vector, so task="batch" (and task="all") additionally require batch - unless labels is a list of two or more files, in which case each cell's file of origin (1, 2, ...) is the batch, the rule run_all applies (see below).

metrics = mtb.evaluate(
    result.output,
    task="all",
    labels=list(mtb.labels_for("D52").values()),   # [cty1.csv, cty2.csv, cty3.csv], in order
    # batch=my_batch_vector                        # overrides the file-of-origin rule
)

Every input can be a path or an in-memory object:

  • output - a numpy.ndarray (cells x dims; a dims x cells array whose other axis matches the label count is transposed for you, with a warning), a pandas.DataFrame, an AnnData (.obsm[obsm], default "X_emb"), a scipy sparse matrix, or a path: .h5 (dataset data, the benchmark's embedding.h5), .h5ad, .npy, .csv / .tsv.
  • labels / batch / clustering - a CSV path (header row; column x, the only column, or the last of two behind a barcode index - pass column= when the file is ambiguous), a list of CSV paths concatenated in that order, a one-entry dict as returned by mtb.labels_for, a 1-D array / Series / Categorical / list, a single-column DataFrame, or - when output is an AnnData - the name of an obs column. Values are compared as strings, so integer codes and names score identically.

Missing labels raises

task="clustering" without labels raises ValueError; task="batch" / "all" without batch (and without a multi-file labels list) raises ValueError too, and a length mismatch says exactly what it saw (input length mismatch: emb has 2863 cells, celltype has 2864). These are programmer errors, not missing optional metrics - see graceful degradation below for the latter.

docs.title: Restricting what is computed
docs.text:
only= names the metrics you want (a collection, not a bare string - that raises TypeError; an unknown name raises ValueError listing the vocabulary, mtb.plot.CLUSTERING_METRICS + mtb.plot.BATCH_METRICS). Everything else is skipped, including the Leiden sweep when no requested metric needs it:

mtb.evaluate(result.output, labels=labels, only={"ARI", "NMI"})        # no Leiden sweep, ~seconds
mtb.evaluate(result.output, task="all", labels=labels, batch=batch,
             only=["ARI", "ASW_batch", "GC"])

slow_metrics=True adds kBET (shells out to R; hours on large datasets).

docs.title: Are my numbers comparable?
docs.text:
The metrics in the shipped tables and the metrics evaluate returns are computed the same way, so yes - provided you feed the same things:

  • labels - the dataset's cty CSV(s), one label per cell in the embedding's cell order. mtb.labels_for(ds) returns them ({"cty": ...} for single-label datasets, {"rna_cty", "atac_cty"} for diagonal, {"cty1", "cty2", ...} per batch); pass the one path, or list(labels_for(ds).values()) in batch order.
  • clustering - omitted, scIB's optimal-resolution Leiden: ten resolutions from 0.2 to 2.0 on the embedding's neighbour graph, keeping the one with the highest NMI against the labels. Pass clustering= to score your own.
  • metrics - the scib.metrics functions; iASW / iF1 score every label (the isolated-label threshold is set to the batch count + 1, so no label is excluded).
  • cLISI / iLISI - need scib's compiled LISI helper (knn_graph.o); when it cannot run, the metric is NaN and the warning contains the exact g++ command that rebuilds it.

docs.title: Batch vector on multi-batch layouts
docs.text:
run_all scores batch metrics against the label file each cell came from: cty1.csv -> 1, cty2.csv -> 2 (cross / mosaic), rna_cty.csv -> 1, atac_cty.csv -> 2 (diagonal) - the winning permutation is recorded in summary.label_order, and summary.batch_source says file_of_origin. Batches within one file (donors inside rna.h5, say) are therefore not represented. When your dataset has them, re-score with the vector it really has - nothing is re-run:

res = mtb.run_all("MYDATA", "cross", out_dir="out/", batch=my_batch_vector)   # at run time, or
res2 = res.rescore(batch=my_batch_vector)          # on the stored outputs; batch_source becomes 'user'
mtb.evaluate(Path(res.results[0]["out_dir"]) / "embedding.h5",               # one stored output
             task="batch", labels=labels, batch=my_batch_vector)

docs.title: Re-runs are stochastic
docs.text: Most methods are non-deterministic, so a re-run does not reproduce the stored decimals. notebooks/results/final_verification.tsv records every verification run (columns method, dataset, category, status, wall_s, ARI, baseline, verdict, note; baseline is the ARI recorded when the method was first verified, verdict is DRIFT when the re-run leaves the tolerance): on D11, 11 of 13 methods re-scored within ~0.02 ARI of their baseline, while VIMCCA moved 0.599 -> 0.695 and Concerto 0.408 -> 0.498. Compare ranks, not decimals, and prefer aggregate="summary" over several datasets when ordering methods.

docs.title: Graceful degradation
docs.text:
A few scIB metrics depend on external machinery that is not always present. Rather than failing the whole evaluation when one optional metric cannot run, evaluate computes each metric defensively: if it raises, the metric is recorded as NaN with a warning, and every other metric still returns.

Metric Needs If unavailable cLISI, iLISI scib's compiled LISI helper NaN + warning (with the rebuild command) kBET R via rpy2, and slow_metrics=True NaN + warning

So on a machine without the LISI binary, a task="clustering" call still gives you real ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, and iF1, only cLISI comes back NaN.

docs.text:

It is a plain DataFrame, so you can save it as the benchmark's metric.csv directly:

docs.title: Closing the loop: tidy -> bubble plot
docs.text:
The wide "Value" frame is the right shape for one run. To compare across methods and datasets, and to draw the scIB-style bubble table from the paper, reshape it to the long frame that plot.bubble and load_results use, with mtb.to_long:

mtb.to_long(value_df, method, dataset, category) -> pd.DataFrame
# columns: metric, value, method, dataset, category

to_long maps each metric name to its canonical form (and raises if two rows collapse onto the same name, so nothing is double-counted), so the result lines up with mtb.load_results and can be concatenated with the stored tables.

import pandas as pd
import multibench as mtb

mine = mtb.to_long(metrics, method="SCALEX", dataset="D28", category="diagonal")
bench = mtb.load_results("diagonal", dataset="D28", source="rerun")   # the package's re-run sweep

fig = mtb.plot.bubble(
    pd.concat([bench, mine]),
    metrics=["ARI", "NMI", "ASW", "GC"],   # this column order, left to right
    title="Diagonal integration, D28 + SCALEX",
    save="bubble.pdf",
)

plot.bubble returns a Matplotlib Figure (circle radius tracks rank, fill tracks value, one Overall bar per metric family). See the plotting tutorial for the full set of options, including published vs re-run tables.

v1 supports metric_set="scib" only

Passing any other metric_set, or a task outside {clustering, batch, all}, raises NotImplementedError. Additional metric sets are planned but not yet wired.

Modality roles and the filenames they resolve to:
    rna              rna.h5      - gene expression
    adt              adt.h5      - surface protein (CITE-seq antibody-derived tags)
    atac             atac.h5     - chromatin accessibility
    atac_gas         atac.h5     - ATAC as GENE-ACTIVITY scores  <-- note: plain atac.h5
    atac_peak        peak.h5     - ATAC as PEAKS                 <-- note: peak.h5, NOT atac.h5
    rna1/rna2/...    rna1.h5, rna2.h5, ... - one file per BATCH (mosaic/cross)
    adt1/adt2/...    adt1.h5, adt2.h5, ... - one file per BATCH (mosaic/cross)
    cty              cty.csv     - cell-type labels, ONE label set (vertical)
    rna_cty / atac_cty rna_cty.csv, atac_cty.csv - one label file PER MODALITY, used when RNA and ATAC come from different cells (diagonal)
    cty1/cty2/...    cty1.csv, cty2.csv, ... - one label file per BATCH (mosaic/cross)

!! ATAC: the role name does NOT guarantee the representation.
   atac_gas resolves to atac_gas.h5 if present, otherwise FALLS BACK
   to atac.h5 - and in the shipped multiome datasets (D12-D17) atac.h5
   contains PEAKS, not gene activity. Only D27/D28 ship a real
   atac_gas.h5. Verified by feature names: 12 atac.h5 files are peaks
   (chr1:3094772-3095489), 2 atac_gas.h5 files are gene activity.
   atac_peak resolves to atac_peak.h5, else peak.h5.
   This matters because methods disagree (lists from the registry;
   see mtb.find_methods(atac=...) / mtb.method_info(m)['atac']):
     need GENE ACTIVITY: SCALEX/scBridge/scMDC/Matilda/VIPCCA/Portal/uniPort/sciCAN/scJoint/UnitedNet/iNMF/online_iNMF/Conos
     need PEAKS:         Multigrate/Seurat_v5/MultiVI/Cobolt/scMVP/scMM/scMoMaT/moETM/MIRA/VIMCCA/SMILE/GLUE/MultiMAP/iPOLNG/StabMap/Seurat_v3/Seurat_WNN
   Feeding the wrong one runs to completion and returns a plausible
   but WRONG embedding - no error.
   Check what you actually have before trusting a cross-dataset result.
   scan() flags the commonest trap in its `caveat` column: an atac_gas
   role that fell back to an atac.h5 whose features are chr:start-end.

MODALITY FILE FORMAT (.h5) - easiest route first:
  mtb.io.to_canonical(src, dst)   converts an .h5ad and writes
  everything below correctly. Prefer it over building the file by hand.
  For a whole dataset in one call (every modality + labels, numbered
  per batch when batch= is given):
    mtb.io.export_dataset(adata, '<data_path>/MYDATA', rna='X',
                          adt='obsm:protein', labels='obs:cell_type')
  Both store matrix/data as float64, gzip-compressed and chunked, like
  the shipped files (a 3000x2000 8%-dense matrix is ~1.5 MB on disk).

  If you do build it yourself, ALL THREE datasets are required:
    matrix/data      the matrix, stored FEATURES x CELLS
    matrix/features  one entry per feature (row of matrix/data)
    matrix/barcodes  one entry per cell    (column of matrix/data)
  e.g. 2,000 genes x 5,000 cells -> matrix/data has shape (2000, 5000),
  matrix/features has 2000 entries and matrix/barcodes has 5000.
  NOTE this is the TRANSPOSE of the scanpy/AnnData convention
  (AnnData.X is cells x genes). scan() rejects a transposed file, and
  a file with only matrix/data fails with a KeyError about 'features'.
Labels are a single-column CSV: one header line (typically 'x'),
then one cell-type label per cell; the evaluator reads the first
column and skips the header.

mosaic: Several batches where only SOME share a modality; a paired batch bridges the others.


ENVIRONMENTS
  Every method runs in its OWN conda env (they need mutually
  incompatible framework versions). scan() checks TWO gates per row -
  files_ok (the inputs are on disk, oriented and labelled) and env_ok
  (that conda env exists) - and marks a method runnable only when both
  pass, so a sweep never starts one that cannot finish.
      multibench env doctor          # what is needed / what is missing
      multibench env install --run   # build them all from lockfiles
      multibench env install --methods X --packed --run   # just one

Then:  mtb.scan('MYDATA')  ->  mtb.run_all('MYDATA', '<category>', out_dir=...)

Each modality file is HDF5 with three datasets:

dataset contents shape matrix/data the matrix, features x cells (n_features, n_cells) matrix/features one name per feature (n_features,) matrix/barcodes one id per cell (n_cells,)

That is the transpose of the AnnData convention (AnnData.X is cells x genes); the mtb.io writers below handle it, and scan() rejects a transposed file at preflight rather than letting a method fail half an hour in. The label CSV is a single column with one header line (typically x) and one label per cell, in the same order as matrix/barcodes of the matching modality file. For ATAC, check which representation a method wants - gene-activity scores or peaks - because the wrong one runs to completion and returns a plausible but wrong embedding. import os, shutil
import h5py
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def subsample_dataset(src_dir, dst_dir, frac=0.6, seed=0):
    """Copy a dataset to a new name, keeping a random fraction of the cells.

    Files sharing a cell count get the SAME kept-cell index, so modality files
    and their label CSVs stay aligned - which is exactly the property your own
    export pipeline must preserve. The output is the canonical layout:
    matrix/data as features x cells, plus matrix/features and matrix/barcodes.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    os.makedirs(dst_dir, exist_ok=True)
    counts, keep = {}, {}
    for fn in sorted(os.listdir(src_dir)):
        p = os.path.join(src_dir, fn)
        if fn.endswith(".h5"):
            with h5py.File(p) as f:
                if "matrix/data" in f:
                    counts[fn] = f["matrix/data"].shape[1]   # features x cells
        elif fn.endswith(".csv"):
            counts[fn] = len(pd.read_csv(p))
    for n in set(counts.values()):
        k = max(50, int(n * frac))
        keep[n] = np.sort(rng.choice(n, size=k, replace=False))
    for fn, n in counts.items():
        sp, dp = os.path.join(src_dir, fn), os.path.join(dst_dir, fn)
        idx = keep[n]
        if fn.endswith(".csv"):
            pd.read_csv(sp).iloc[idx].to_csv(dp, index=False)
        else:
            with h5py.File(sp) as f, h5py.File(dp, "w") as g:
                grp = g.create_group("matrix")
                grp.create_dataset("data", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/data"])[:, idx])
                if "matrix/features" in f:
                    grp.create_dataset("features", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/features"]))
                if "matrix/barcodes" in f:
                    grp.create_dataset("barcodes", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/barcodes"])[idx])
    return dst_dir

docs.title: Mosaic integration¶
docs.text:
Mosaic integration has several batches where only some share a modality - an RNA-only batch, an ATAC-only batch, and a paired batch that bridges them. Which methods apply depends on the exact per-batch pattern, so scan() is the source of truth for each dataset.

Reference dataset: D45 (32,151 cells). The stored results shipped with these notebooks were produced on it, so every table here reproduces.

docs.title: 1. Install¶
docs.text: Two layers: the multibench package (~2 MB) and the conda environments of the methods you run. On Colab, run the first cell and let the kernel restart once - then keep running from the next cell. Sections 2-3 (running methods) need the environments and a Linux runtime with the disk for them; sections 4-5 (stored results, reference) need only the package.

docs.title: 2. Run the analysis¶
docs.text: One call is the whole pipeline: resolve each method's inputs, run it in its own conda env, load the embeddings, score them with scIB metrics. Here StabMap, scMoMaT (on D46, whose layout fits these methods; mosaic layouts vary per dataset). Both run in minutes to tens of minutes on D46 - run_sec in the summary is the measured time on our host.

docs.title: 3. Your own data¶
docs.text: The same three calls - scan, run_all, plot - on a folder the package has never seen. A dataset is a folder of flat files named by category:

docs.title: 4. Reading stored results¶
docs.text: Section 2 ran two methods; the package ships the full sweep for D45 - every wired method at default settings, hours of compute - so the paper's figures reproduce from stored results in seconds. load_results reads them back as the tidy frame mtb.plot.bubble takes; source="rerun" selects the package's own re-execution (the tables behind this notebook), "published" the paper's tables, and every row says which it came from in its source column.

docs.title: What runs on a dataset, and why not¶
docs.text: scan inspects a folder and reports every runnable method - and for the rest, the exact reason (missing file, missing environment, wrong layout). Nothing executes.

docs.title: What each method exposes for tuning¶
docs.text: method_info(m)["supports"] lists a method's variants with how many hyperparameters each exposes on its command line; mtb.params_for(m, CATEGORY, modalities) names them. An empty tunable is honest: many upstream scripts hardcode their hyperparameters, and this package never edits upstream code.

docs.title: What the registry knows about a method, and how to cite it¶
docs.text: method_info carries the upstream reference, repository and version next to the run metadata (verbose=True adds the long audit notes); mtb.cite emits the benchmark entry plus one per method you ran.

docs.title: The metrics¶
docs.text:
Two families, matching the paper's grouping. All are higher = better, on [0, 1] except ARI (slightly negative at chance level).

family metrics what they measure clustering / bio-conservation ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1, cLISI does the embedding separate the annotated cell types? batch correction ASW_batch, GC, iLISI (+ opt-in kBET) are the batches mixed within each cell type?

Batch metrics appear only when the dataset has real batches - their absence on a single-batch dataset is correct, not missing data. kBET is opt-in (mtb.evaluate(..., slow_metrics=True)) because it is much slower than the rest.

docs.title: Coverage of the paper¶
docs.text: scan() answers "what runs on this dataset"; this answers how many of the methods the paper benchmarks for mosaic the package wires at all.

docs.title: Troubleshooting¶
docs.text: symptom meaning fix files_ok False: input files not found a required file is absent the reason names the exact file and lists what IS in the folder env_ok False that method's conda env is not built the reason carries the one-method multibench env install ... command ... looks like cells x features matrix stored transposed re-export with mtb.io.to_canonical / export_dataset a method FAILs in seconds wrong input representation or layout read res.failures.iloc[0]["error"] - the full command line and stderr tail are there a method TIMEOUTs slow, not broken raise timeout=; runtime tiers in scan are measured, not guessed label_order_confidence low several label files fit the cell count check label_order_candidates in the record batch metrics scored against the wrong batches batch_source="file_of_origin" is the label-file rule res.rescore(batch=my_vector) re-scores the stored outputs without re-running

docs.title: Why is UINMF not in mosaic?¶
docs.text: Two verified blockers, recorded in the registry: its upstream script derives the second batch's unshared features from the FIRST batch's object (harmless when both unshared blocks are the same modality, fatal otherwise), and its two-batch shape fits no mosaic dataset shipped here. A method scan() reports as runnable must actually run, so it is deliberately not offered.

docs.title: Load & plot results
docs.text:
scMultiBench ships the published benchmark metric tables from Liu, Ding et al. (Nature Methods 2025) and the package's own re-run sweeps, alongside the code that drew the figures. This tutorial covers the two functions you need to turn those tables into a publication-ready panel: mtb.load_results reads the stored metric tables into one tidy long frame, and mtb.plot.bubble renders the scIB-style bubble table the paper uses.

TL;DR

import multibench as mtb

df = mtb.load_results("vertical", dataset="D11")                  # the paper's table
fig = mtb.plot.bubble(df, metrics=["ARI", "NMI", "ASW", "cLISI"],
                      title="Vertical integration, D11", save="d11.pdf")

The same panel from the shell:

terminal
multibench plot bubble --category vertical --dataset D11 \
    --metrics ARI,NMI,ASW,cLISI --out d11.pdf

docs.title: Step 1, Load a tidy results frame
docs.text:
mtb.load_results walks the stored result tree and returns a single long-format pandas.DataFrame with seven columns - metric, value, method, dataset, category, clustering, source. One row per (method, dataset, metric) cell. This is the shape every downstream function (plot.bubble, plot.bar, recommend, your own groupby/pivot) expects.

import multibench as mtb

df = mtb.load_results(
    category="vertical",      # vertical | diagonal | mosaic | cross; None -> every category
    task=None,                # None/"all" -> every metric; "clustering" / "batch" -> one family
    metric_set="scib",        # only "scib" is wired in v1
    dataset="D11",            # None -> every dataset; a list -> several
    method=None,              # None -> every method present; a name or list (alias tolerant)
    metric=None,              # None -> every metric; or ["ARI", "NMI"]
    clustering="default",     # default | louvain | kmeans
    source="published",       # published | rerun | both
)
df.head()
#   metric     value      method dataset  category clustering     source
# 0    NMI  0.792936  Multigrate     D11  vertical    default  published
# 1    ARI  0.759446  Multigrate     D11  vertical    default  published
# 2    ASW  0.656011  Multigrate     D11  vertical    default  published
# ...

docs.title: Category tokens
docs.text:
scMultiBench groups its 40 integration methods into four integration categories. Pass the clean token; the loader maps it to the (space-named) folder on disk for you. A typo raises ValueError listing the valid ones.

Token Integration setting Modalities vertical Paired, the same cells profiled in every modality RNA+ADT, RNA+ATAC, RNA+ADT+ATAC diagonal Unpaired, separate batches bridged by shared features RNA batch + ATAC batch mosaic Overlapping modalities joined through a bridge mixed cross Several fully-matched datasets integrated together matched

docs.title: Published vs re-run tables
docs.text:
Two sources ship in the package, and the source column of every frame says which one a row came from:

source= What it is Datasets "published" (default) the paper's scIB tables (multibench/result/scib_metric/) vertical 23, diagonal 18, cross 6; none for mosaic (FileNotFoundError pointing at source="rerun") "rerun" the package's own sweeps - every wired method at default settings, the tables behind the category tutorials (multibench/result/rerun/long_all_<dataset>.csv, source="rerun-0.2.1") vertical D11/D11s, diagonal D28/D28s, mosaic D45/D45s, cross D52/D52s "both" the concatenation tell them apart by source

The two can differ for the same method and dataset: methods are stochastic, the published sweep ran on other hardware, and the published tables are partial (vertical ships 8 of the paper's methods; cross mostly one method per dataset) while the re-runs cover every wired method for their dataset. Cite the published numbers; use the re-runs to check reproducibility and to compare against your own run, and compare ranks rather than decimals (see Are my numbers comparable?). mtb.results_coverage(category) lists which (dataset, method, clustering, source) combinations exist; mtb.available_datasets(category, source=...) lists the loadable dataset ids.

cov = mtb.results_coverage("cross")
cov[cov.dataset == "D52"].groupby("source").method.nunique()   # published 1, rerun-0.2.1 8

docs.title: Clustering variants
docs.text:
scIB clustering metrics depend on the upstream clustering. The published tree stores up to three variants per (dataset, method); pick one with clustering=:

Value Reads Meaning "default" metric.csv the paper's default clustering (Leiden), with corrected ASW/iASW/iF1 coalesced in "louvain" metric_louvain.csv Louvain re-clustering "kmeans" metric_kmeans.csv k-means re-clustering

Which variants ship, per category

diagonal ships all three variants for all 18 datasets. vertical ships louvain for a single (dataset, method) pair (D3 / Concerto) and no kmeans; cross ships neither. Asking for a variant that is not there raises FileNotFoundError naming the file it looked for; point result_path= at a tree that contains it, or keep clustering="default". The re-run sweeps are default only. A result directory named <method>_louvain is reported under the method's canonical id with clustering="louvain" - no method id ever ends in _louvain.

Metric names and method ids are canonicalised

Both metric= and the returned metric column are passed through catalog.canonical_metric, so you can filter with the clean scIB names - ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1, cLISI (clustering) and ASW_batch, GC, iLISI, kBET (batch) - regardless of how the underlying CSV spelled them. Likewise method= accepts any alias of a method id ("mofa+" -> MOFA2, "Seurat(WNN)" -> Seurat_WNN). A filter that matches nothing returns an empty frame with a UserWarning listing what is present, so concatenating several calls never breaks on one typo.

These are stored tables, not a live run

To score your own run instead, compute metrics with mtb.evaluate and reshape the wide frame with mtb.to_long(value_df, method, dataset, category) - it emits the same long frame, so it drops straight into plot.bubble next to a stored table. result_path= also accepts a single long CSV (one you saved with to_csv, or a run_all output's long.csv) and reads it back with source="user" unless the file carries its own.

docs.title: Step 2, Render the scIB bubble table
docs.text:
mtb.plot.bubble takes the long frame and draws the scIB-style bubble table - the grid of circles the paper uses to rank methods. It returns a matplotlib.Figure.

fig = mtb.plot.bubble(
    df,
    metrics=["ARI", "NMI", "ASW", "cLISI"],   # column order, left to right (within each family)
    methods=None,                              # None -> every method in df; unknown names raise
    order=None,                                # None -> best first; a list pins those rows on top
    aggregate="dataset",                       # "dataset" | "summary"
    cmap=None,                                 # override the first family's colour ramp
    title="Vertical integration, D11",
    save="d11_bubble.pdf",                     # also returns the Figure
    show_language=True,                        # Py / R chip per row, 'L' badge for label-consuming methods
    require_complete=False,                    # summary: keep only methods present in every dataset
    overall="rank",                            # how the across-dataset Overall is formed (see below)
)

How to read it:

  • Each row is a method, each column a metric. Metrics are grouped into the paper's task families - blues for DR & clustering, greens for batch correction - and each family is led by an Overall bar. Rows are ordered by the mean of the family Overall scores, best at the top.
  • Circle fill ~ value - darker = higher, on a per-column min-max scale.
  • Circle radius ~ rank - bigger = better in that column (0.85 * sqrt(rank / n); ties take the maximum rank, matching the original R ties.method="max").
  • The family Overall bar - within one dataset, minmax(mean over the family's metrics of per-metric max-rank); length and fill both carry it.
  • Legend - a Score colour ramp per family always; the Rank circle-size legend only under aggregate="dataset" (summary panels draw bars); a dash marks a metric that was not computed for that method (n/a).
  • A ? chip marks a method that is not in the registry (your own), an L badge a method that consumes cell-type labels - supervised, so its scores are not comparable with the unsupervised rows.

docs.title: Individual vs. summary panels
docs.text:
The aggregate argument decides what a row's numbers mean.

aggregate=\"dataset\" (individual)aggregate=\"summary\" (across datasets) 
# one dataset -> raw metric values are plotted directly
df = mtb.load_results("vertical", dataset="D11")
fig = mtb.plot.bubble(df, metrics=["ARI", "NMI", "ASW", "cLISI"])

The default. Fill encodes the actual metric value for that dataset. If the frame happens to hold several datasets, values are averaged per (method, metric) first, a UserWarning says so, and the row labels carry the dataset ids.

# all vertical datasets -> rank within each, then average ranks
df = mtb.load_results("vertical")          # no dataset= -> all
fig = mtb.plot.bubble(df, metrics=["ARI", "NMI", "ASW", "cLISI"],
                      aggregate="summary", require_complete=True,
                      title="Vertical integration, summary")

Ranks methods within each dataset per metric, then averages those ranks across datasets and draws them as bars - the cross-dataset leaderboard, not a raw mean of incommensurable scores. A method absent from a dataset scores rank 0 there (the paper's rule), which pulls it down; a UserWarning lists such methods, and require_complete=True restricts the panel to methods present in every dataset instead.

The across-dataset Overall: overall=

Two formulas exist and they can order methods differently on the same frame. "rank" (bubble's default, the paper's summary rule): minmax(mean over metrics of max-rank(mean over datasets of within-dataset max-rank)) - absence counts as rank 0. "mean_overall" (bar's default): mean over datasets of minmax(mean over metrics of within-dataset max-rank) - each dataset gets its own min-max-scaled overall, averaged over the datasets the method was actually run on (absence skipped). Pass the same overall= to plot.bubble and plot.bar to get the same ordering; the formula in use is printed on the figure.

Pinning the row order

Pass order=[...] (a list of method ids) to put those rows first, in that order - handy when you want a fixed method order shared across several figures; unlisted methods follow, best first. order= only reorders (an unknown name raises ValueError); methods=[...] subsets the frame before anything is ranked, and metrics= sets the column order within each family. Duplicate (method[, dataset], metric) rows raise rather than being silently averaged - name variants distinctly.

docs.title: Audit the numbers before drawing
docs.text: mtb.plot.build_table(df, ...) returns the BubbleTable behind the figure (methods in row order, overall, matrix, raw, norm, ranks, blocks), so ranks can be read programmatically - e.g. the position of your own method: mtb.plot.build_table(allruns).methods.index("MyMethod") + 1. mtb.plot.render(table) draws it.

docs.title: Summary bars
docs.text: mtb.plot.bar(df, group="clustering" | "batch", overall=..., top=N, save=...) draws one bar per method with its across-dataset Overall - the benchmark's two summary panels - with one dot per dataset behind each bar (under overall="mean_overall") so a uniformly good method is distinguishable from one that wins a single dataset.

docs.title: A concrete example, a vertical panel
docs.text:
Reproduce one vertical-integration panel end to end, then add your own method:

reproduce_d11.py
import pandas as pd
import multibench as mtb

# 1. stored table for one dataset - the re-run sweep covers every wired method
bench = mtb.load_results("vertical", dataset="D11", source="rerun")

# 2. your own run, scored with the same metrics (see Evaluate a run)
mine = mtb.to_long(mtb.evaluate(emb, labels=mtb.labels_for("D11")["cty"]),
                   method="MyMethod", dataset="D11", category="vertical")

# 3. bubble table, four clustering metrics, saved to PDF
fig = mtb.plot.bubble(
    pd.concat([bench, mine]),
    metrics=["ARI", "NMI", "ASW", "cLISI"],
    title="Vertical integration, D11 + MyMethod",
    save="d11_vertical.pdf",
)
print(mtb.plot.build_table(pd.concat([bench, mine])).methods.index("MyMethod") + 1)   # its rank

The returned fig is a plain matplotlib.Figure, so you can keep tweaking it (fig.axes[0]...), embed it in a multi-panel layout, or re-save at another DPI.

docs.title: CLI equivalent
docs.text:
The same figure without writing any Python:

terminal
multibench plot bubble \
    --category vertical --dataset D11 --source rerun \
    --metrics ARI,NMI,ASW,cLISI \
    --out d11_vertical.pdf

multibench plot accepts --aggregate dataset|summary, --overall rank|mean_overall, --require-complete, --methods, --title, --input long.csv (your own long table, or a run_all output directory, instead of --category), bar with --group clustering|batch, and writes whatever format --out's extension implies (.pdf, .png, ...). It calls load_results and plot.bubble / plot.bar under the hood, so the result is identical to the script above.

Visual fidelity

The bubble table is a matplotlib reproduction of scIB's original R tables (helpers.R / scIB_knit_table.R). The numeric encoding - min-max fills, max-rank radii, the overall bars - is ported verbatim, so rankings and shadings match; the rendering is visually faithful within tolerance rather than a pixel-exact clone of the R figure.

Next: see the API reference for the full load_results, plot.bubble, evaluate, and to_long signatures.

docs.title: Run a method
docs.text:
scMultiBench runs the original, unmodified method scripts from the reference repository - it never edits them. mtb.run reads a method's declaration from the registry, picks the right variant from the inputs you pass, builds the exact command line, runs it inside that method's own conda environment, and loads the typed output back into Python. (mtb.run_all does this for every method that fits a dataset folder, and scores the outputs - the category tutorials are built on it; this page is the single-method call underneath.)

TL;DR

import multibench as mtb

mtb.data.fetch("D28")                          # 137 MB reference dataset; no-op when present
res = mtb.run(
    "SCALEX", "diagonal",
    inputs=mtb.inputs_for("D28", "SCALEX", "diagonal"),   # {'rna': .../D28/rna.h5, 'atac_gas': .../D28/atac_gas.h5}
    out_dir="runs/scalex_d28",
)
res.output.shape   # -> (11014, 10)  joint embedding: 6,408 RNA + 4,606 ATAC cells x latent dims

docs.title: The run model
docs.text:
Each method is declared once in the registry (multibench/engine/methods.yaml) as a MethodSpec. A spec lists the categories and tasks the method supports, the conda env it needs, and one variant per (category, modality-set) it can handle. A single mtb.run call walks this path:

  1. Look up the spec for method and collect the modality roles from your inputs (auxiliary roles like data_dir are ignored here).
  2. Select the variant whose when: matches (category, modalities). The match is exact on the set of modality roles - {"rna", "atac_gas"} selects the diagonal RNA + gene-activity variant, not the vertical one.
  3. Preflight the environment: with the default cmd_template, a missing conda env raises EnvironmentError naming the install command before anything is written.
  4. Convert inputs to the canonical scMultiBench .h5 (unless convert=False) into a per-run inputs/ folder.
  5. Build the command - [interpreter, entrypoint, *args, *params] - with the entrypoint resolved against the reference repo_path.
  6. Wrap and execute via cmd_template (default conda run -n <env> {cmd}) in the per-run out_dir working directory.
  7. Load the output by its declared kind (e.g. an embedding ndarray) into a RunResult.

Each method needs its own conda environment

The env each method needs is declared in the registry - for SCALEX it is scmb_torch (see mtb.method_info("SCALEX")["env"]) - and it must exist on your machine. Build it from the committed lockfile (or a prebuilt archive) with multibench env install --methods SCALEX --packed --run; multibench env doctor lists what exists and what is missing. mtb.run shells out with conda run -n <env> ...; if the env is missing the preflight raises EnvironmentError with that install command.

docs.title: Inputs: roles and format flexibility
docs.text:
inputs is a dict mapping each modality role to a file path (or an in-memory AnnData). Roles are the method's own argument names from the registry - for SCALEX's diagonal variant they are rna and atac_gas (gene-activity scores derived from ATAC). For a benchmark dataset, mtb.inputs_for(dataset, method, category) resolves them for you (and check=True verifies the files exist, are oriented features x cells and have one label per cell).

You do not have to pre-convert your data. By default mtb.run routes every modality input through mtb.io.to_canonical, which adapts common formats to the canonical scMultiBench .h5 (HDF5 with matrix/data as features x cells, matrix/features, matrix/barcodes; sparse matrices are streamed, the file is gzip-compressed):

Input you pass Handled by to_canonical .h5ad / .h5mu anndata / mudata readers (mod= picks the MuData modality) .csv / .tsv parsed to a matrix (cells x features) .loom anndata.read_loom in-memory AnnData used directly (layer= / obsm= select the matrix) already-canonical .h5 passed through unchanged 
# both inputs become canonical .h5 before the method sees them; the D28
# files are already canonical, so to_canonical passes them through unchanged
mtb.run(
    "SCALEX", "diagonal",
    inputs={"rna": "data/D28/rna.h5", "atac_gas": "data/D28/atac_gas.h5"},
    out_dir="runs/scalex_d28",
)

Pass convert=False when your inputs are already in the exact layout the method expects and you want scMultiBench to hand the paths through verbatim:

mtb.run(..., convert=False)   # no format adaptation; paths used as-is

docs.title: Your own data as a dataset folder
docs.text:
For run_all / scan (and for inputs_for) the inputs live in a dataset folder laid out by category - mtb.describe_layout(category) prints the contract. One call writes it from an AnnData or MuData:

import anndata as ad
a = ad.read_h5ad("my_citeseq.h5ad")                 # X = RNA, obsm['protein'] = ADT, obs['celltype']
mtb.io.export_dataset(a, "data/MYCITE", rna="X", adt="obsm:protein", labels="obs:celltype")
#   -> data/MYCITE/rna.h5, adt.h5, cty.csv; batch="obs:sample" writes rna1.h5/cty1.csv ... per batch
mtb.io.from_mudata(mdata, "data/MYMULTIOME", rna="rna", atac="atac", atac_kind="peak", labels="rna:celltype")
mtb.scan("MYCITE", "vertical", data_path="data")    # files_ok / env_ok per method, with reasons

Or file by file - to_canonical(src, "data/MYDIAG", modality="rna") picks the canonical filename for the modality, mtb.io.write_labels(labels, path) writes the single-column cty CSV, and read_canonical is the inverse (canonical .h5 -> AnnData, cells x genes). The modality argument is validated, and for ATAC it is the one place you say whether the matrix is peaks or gene activity - the two are not interchangeable, see the ATAC note printed by describe_layout.

docs.title: Inspecting variants before you run
docs.text:
Use mtb.method_info to see which categories, tasks, environment, and variant entrypoints a method declares - supports lists, per variant, the modality roles it expects and whether it needs labels.

info = mtb.method_info("SCALEX")
info["env"], info["atac"], info["needs_labels"]   # ('scmb_torch', 'gene_activity', False)
info["supports"]
# [{'category': 'diagonal', 'modalities': ['rna', 'atac_gas'],
#   'output_kind': 'embedding', 'n_tunable': 0, 'needs_labels': False}]

If the (category, modalities) you pass has no matching variant, mtb.run raises a KeyError that lists every (category, modality-set) the method does support, so the fix is usually to adjust your inputs keys.

status tells you what is wired

Every registry method has status: "verified": its command template was cross-checked against the real entrypoint and executed end to end on a reference dataset - notebooks/results/final_verification.tsv in the repository records each run with its ARI, the baseline ARI from first verification and a verdict (DRIFT when a stochastic re-run leaves the tolerance).

docs.title: Validated example: SCALEX diagonal integration on D28
docs.text:
This is a real, GPU-validated run (2,233 s on our host - mtb.runtime_hint("SCALEX")). SCALEX performs diagonal integration (unpaired modalities bridged by shared features): an RNA population (rna) and an ATAC population summarised as gene-activity scores (atac_gas) from dataset D28, which mtb.data.fetch("D28") downloads (137 MB).

run_scalex_d28.py
import multibench as mtb

mtb.data.fetch("D28")
res = mtb.run(
    "SCALEX",
    category="diagonal",
    task="clustering",
    inputs=mtb.inputs_for("D28", "SCALEX", "diagonal", check=True),
    out_dir="/abs/path/runs/scalex_d28",
)

print(res.output.shape)   # -> (11014, 10)   joint embedding (RNA + ATAC cells x latent dims)
print(res.cmd)            # the exact argv that ran, including the conda wrapper

Use absolute paths for inputs and out_dir

The method script runs with out_dir as its working directory (step 6 above), and out_dir is also passed to the script as its save path. So a relative out_dir (or relative inputs) is resolved against the subprocess cwd, not your shell's cwd, which makes the outputs land in the wrong place. inputs_for returns absolute paths; pass an absolute out_dir too. No cmd_template is needed: the default conda run -n {env} {cmd} fills {env} from the spec (scmb_torch for SCALEX), so the run lands in the right conda env automatically.

mtb.run returns a RunResult dataclass:

Field Type What it holds method str the method id you ran out_dir Path the per-run working directory cmd list[str] the exact wrapped command line that executed output object the primary loaded output, here an embedding ndarray extra dict any additional declared outputs, keyed by filename stdout / stderr str captured subprocess streams 
res.output            # numpy ndarray, shape (11014, 10), the joint embedding
res.extra             # {} for SCALEX (no extra outputs)
res.cmd[:3]           # [<conda>, 'run', '-n']  -> the cmd_template wrapper

The embedding flows straight into evaluation and plotting. D28's labels are two files - one per modality, because the RNA and ATAC cells differ - and passing both as a list makes each cell's file of origin the batch for the batch metrics (see Evaluate a run):

labels = mtb.labels_for("D28")                      # {'atac_cty': ..., 'rna_cty': ...}
metrics = mtb.evaluate(res.output, category="diagonal", task="all",
                       labels=[labels["rna_cty"], labels["atac_cty"]])   # SCALEX stacks RNA cells, then ATAC

(run_all finds that order for you and records it as summary.label_order; for a single mtb.run you state it.)

docs.title: Choosing a cmd_template
docs.text:
cmd_template decides how the built command is executed; {cmd} is the placeholder for the argv. The default targets the method's declared env:

cmd_template = "conda run -n {env} {cmd}"   # default; {env} filled from the spec

Override it to run elsewhere, e.g. an explicit env name, a Singularity container, or an HPC scheduler wrapper (the env preflight is skipped - you own the environment then):

Explicit conda envSingularity / ApptainerRun in the current env 
mtb.run(..., cmd_template="conda run -n scmb_torch {cmd}")

mtb.run(..., cmd_template="singularity exec multibench.sif {cmd}")

mtb.run(..., cmd_template="{cmd}")   # no wrapper, use the active interpreter

repo_path points at the checkout of the reference scMultiBench method scripts; it defaults to config.DEFAULT.repo_path (auto-provisioned on first run). The variant entrypoint (e.g. tools_scripts/SCALEX/main_SCALEX.py) is resolved relative to it.

docs.title: Reading other output kinds
docs.text:
The primary output is loaded by its declared kind. embedding / imputed / markers / graph outputs come back as numpy arrays; labels as a list of strings; coords as a path you handle yourself. Any additional files a variant declares land in res.extra, keyed by filename.

Graph-output methods do not return an embedding

A few methods emit a cell-graph rather than a coordinate embedding - notably scMoMaT, MIRA, and Seurat_WNN. For these, res.output is the graph representation, not a (cells x dims) embedding, and downstream steps that assume an embedding (e.g. ASW-style metrics) will not apply directly. mtb.method_info(method)["supports"] names each variant's output_kind; run_all scores scMoMaT through the UMAP it also writes (CHAIN_OK_GRAPH_METHOD) and reports Seurat_WNN as RUN_OK_NO_EMBEDDING.

docs.title: Spatial registration
docs.text:
PASTE, PASTE2, SPIRAL and GPSA (task registration, category cross) align spatial slices; their output is aligned coordinates, not an embedding. They take a directory of slices instead of modality files - the role is data_dir, scan() shows their modalities as (data_dir), and you pass no modalities to run_all / inputs_for:

<data_path>/MYVISIUM/            (or <data_path>/MYVISIUM/processed/)
    slice_0.h5ad  slice_1.h5ad  ...   one AnnData per slice, >= 2

import os, shutil
import h5py
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def subsample_dataset(src_dir, dst_dir, frac=0.6, seed=0):
    """Copy a dataset to a new name, keeping a random fraction of the cells.

    Files sharing a cell count get the SAME kept-cell index, so modality files
    and their label CSVs stay aligned - which is exactly the property your own
    export pipeline must preserve. The output is the canonical layout:
    matrix/data as features x cells, plus matrix/features and matrix/barcodes.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    os.makedirs(dst_dir, exist_ok=True)
    counts, keep = {}, {}
    for fn in sorted(os.listdir(src_dir)):
        p = os.path.join(src_dir, fn)
        if fn.endswith(".h5"):
            with h5py.File(p) as f:
                if "matrix/data" in f:
                    counts[fn] = f["matrix/data"].shape[1]   # features x cells
        elif fn.endswith(".csv"):
            counts[fn] = len(pd.read_csv(p))
    for n in set(counts.values()):
        k = max(50, int(n * frac))
        keep[n] = np.sort(rng.choice(n, size=k, replace=False))
    for fn, n in counts.items():
        sp, dp = os.path.join(src_dir, fn), os.path.join(dst_dir, fn)
        idx = keep[n]
        if fn.endswith(".csv"):
            pd.read_csv(sp).iloc[idx].to_csv(dp, index=False)
        else:
            with h5py.File(sp) as f, h5py.File(dp, "w") as g:
                grp = g.create_group("matrix")
                grp.create_dataset("data", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/data"])[:, idx])
                if "matrix/features" in f:
                    grp.create_dataset("features", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/features"]))
                if "matrix/barcodes" in f:
                    grp.create_dataset("barcodes", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/barcodes"])[idx])
    return dst_dir

docs.title: Vertical integration¶
docs.text:
Vertical integration fuses several modalities measured in the same cells (here CITE-seq: RNA + surface protein). Cells are already matched, so the task is combining modalities, not aligning cells.

Reference dataset: D11 (2,864 cells). The stored results shipped with these notebooks were produced on it, so every table here reproduces.

docs.title: 1. Install¶
docs.text: Two layers: the multibench package (~2 MB) and the conda environments of the methods you run. On Colab, run the first cell and let the kernel restart once - then keep running from the next cell. Sections 2-3 (running methods) need the environments and a Linux runtime with the disk for them; sections 4-5 (stored results, reference) need only the package.

docs.title: 2. Run the analysis¶
docs.text: One call is the whole pipeline: resolve each method's inputs, run it in its own conda env, load the embeddings, score them with scIB metrics. Here Matilda, sciPENN, scMM. Matilda at 5 epochs is quick - run_sec in the summary is the measured time on our host.

docs.title: 3. Your own data¶
docs.text: The same three calls - scan, run_all, plot - on a folder the package has never seen. A dataset is a folder of flat files named by category:

docs.title: 4. Reading stored results¶
docs.text: Section 2 ran three methods; the package ships the full sweep for D11 - every wired method at default settings, hours of compute - so the paper's figures reproduce from stored results in seconds. load_results reads them back as the tidy frame mtb.plot.bubble takes; source="rerun" selects the package's own re-execution (the tables behind this notebook), "published" the paper's tables, and every row says which it came from in its source column.

docs.title: What runs on a dataset, and why not¶
docs.text: scan inspects a folder and reports every runnable method - and for the rest, the exact reason (missing file, missing environment, wrong layout). Nothing executes.

docs.title: What each method exposes for tuning¶
docs.text: method_info(m)["supports"] lists a method's variants with how many hyperparameters each exposes on its command line; mtb.params_for(m, CATEGORY, modalities) names them. An empty tunable is honest: many upstream scripts hardcode their hyperparameters, and this package never edits upstream code.

docs.title: What the registry knows about a method, and how to cite it¶
docs.text: method_info carries the upstream reference, repository and version next to the run metadata (verbose=True adds the long audit notes); mtb.cite emits the benchmark entry plus one per method you ran.

docs.title: The metrics¶
docs.text:
Two families, matching the paper's grouping. All are higher = better, on [0, 1] except ARI (slightly negative at chance level).

family metrics what they measure clustering / bio-conservation ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1, cLISI does the embedding separate the annotated cell types? batch correction ASW_batch, GC, iLISI (+ opt-in kBET) are the batches mixed within each cell type?

Batch metrics appear only when the dataset has real batches - their absence on a single-batch dataset is correct, not missing data. kBET is opt-in (mtb.evaluate(..., slow_metrics=True)) because it is much slower than the rest.

docs.title: Coverage of the paper¶
docs.text: scan() answers "what runs on this dataset"; this answers how many of the methods the paper benchmarks for vertical the package wires at all.

docs.text: symptom meaning fix files_ok False: input files not found a required file is absent the reason names the exact file and lists what IS in the folder env_ok False that method's conda env is not built the reason carries the one-method multibench env install ... command ... looks like cells x features matrix stored transposed re-export with mtb.io.to_canonical / export_dataset a method FAILs in seconds wrong input representation or layout read res.failures.iloc[0]["error"] - the full command line and stderr tail are there a method TIMEOUTs slow, not broken raise timeout=; runtime tiers in scan are measured, not guessed label_order_confidence low several label files fit the cell count check label_order_candidates in the record batch metrics scored against the wrong batches batch_source="file_of_origin" is the label-file rule res.rescore(batch=my_vector) re-scores the stored outputs without re-running
